UPPSC Prelims 2025

Quick-revision notes, rewritten as handwritten study notes.

These notes cover the whole "Quick Revision for UPPSC Prelims 2025 (English)" PDF, organised as Subject → Chapter → Topic → Subtopic. Each heading carries its p. 12 tag: the PDF page number where the material appears (the PDF has 163 pages; pp. 1–2 and the section cover pages 18, 35, 63, 81, 93, 116 and 136 carry no notes, and p. 163 is an advertisement).

Facts are kept as the source states them, including its time context (2025 edition; Census figures are 2011). Where the machine-translated source is garbled, contradicts itself or looks wrong or outdated, a Source check note says so rather than silently changing it. All source checks are listed at the end.

Each chapter opens with a chapter map (click a box to jump to that topic) and ends with a chapter recap. Diagrams marked ◈ explain relationships; those with a Hide labels button double as label tests. Every topic ends with Test your memory, whose answers stay hidden until you choose Reveal answer. When printed, the answers move to a separate answer key at the end.

Ancient Indian History

From the Stone Age and the Indus Valley through the Vedic age, Jainism and Buddhism, the Mauryas, Guptas and the southern dynasties. The source is a set of quick-revision lists, grouped here by theme.

Periods of History, Sources, Travellers and Eras

Periods of History

Historians divide the past by how much written evidence exists.

Prehistoric period
The period for which there is no written evidence.
Protohistoric period
Evidence of a script is present but still undeciphered (unread).
Historical period
Written evidence is present.
Test your memory

  1. What distinguishes the protohistoric period from the prehistoric period?

    A script exists but is undeciphered. Prehistory has no written evidence at all. p. 3

  2. Which period is defined by the presence of readable written evidence?

    The historical period. p. 3

  3. A culture has a script that nobody can yet read. Which period does it belong to?

    Protohistoric. p. 3

Important Facts about the Puranas

  • The best systematic description of Indian historical stories is found in the Puranas.
  • Author: Lomaharsha Rishi or his son Ugrasrava.
  • Number of Puranas: 18.
  • Genealogy of kings is found in only five: Matsya, Vayu, Vishnu, Brahmanda, Bhagavata Purana.
  • Oldest and most authentic Purana: Matsya Purana.
  • Mention of the Maurya dynasty: Vishnu Purana.
  • Mention of the Gupta dynasty: Vayu Purana.
  • Mention of the Satavahana dynasty: Matsya Purana.
  • Details of agriculture along with monarchy: Agni Purana.
Source check Source reads “Brahman” in the list of five; likely means “Brahmanda” Purana.
Learning aid “Vishnu–Maurya, Vayu–Gupta, Matsya–Satavahana”: V-M, V-G, M-S. (not from source)
Test your memory

  1. How many Puranas are there, and who is credited with composing them?

    18; Lomaharsha Rishi or his son Ugrasrava. p. 5

  2. Which Purana describes the Maurya dynasty, which the Gupta and which the Satavahana?

    Vishnu – Maurya; Vayu – Gupta; Matsya – Satavahana. p. 5

  3. Which Purana is considered the oldest and most authentic?

    Matsya Purana. p. 5

  4. Name the five Puranas that give the genealogy of kings.

    Matsya, Vayu, Vishnu, Brahmanda, Bhagavata. p. 5

Major Eras (Samvats)

  1. 57 BCE Vikram Samvat – started by King Vikramaditya of Ujjain.
  2. 78 CE Shaka Samvat – Kushana ruler Kanishka, after victory over the Shakas.
  3. 248 CE Kalachuri Samvat – Abhira ruler Ishwarsena.
  4. 319 CE Gupta Samvat – Chandragupta I.
  5. 606 CE Harsha Samvat – Harshavardhana of Kannauj.
  6. 622 CE Hijri Samvat – in memory of Prophet Muhammad’s journey from Mecca to Medina.
  7. 825 CE Kollam Samvat – by Shankaracharya in Malabar (as per source).
  8. 1113 CE Singh/Siddha Samvat – Chalukya Jayasimha Siddharaja.
  9. 1190 CE Lakshman Samvat – Lakshman Sen of the Sena dynasty, Bengal.
  10. 1583 CE Ilahi Samvat – Mughal emperor Akbar.
  11. 1673 CE Rajashaka – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.
Source check Attribution of the Kollam era to Shankaracharya is as given in the source; this attribution is doubtful.
Test your memory

  1. Which era began in 78 CE and who started it?

    Shaka Samvat – Kushana ruler Kanishka, after victory over the Shakas. p. 8

    Vikram (57 BCE) → Gupta (319 CE) → Harsha (606 CE) → Hijri (622 CE). p. 8–9

  3. Who started the Ilahi Samvat, and in which year?

    Akbar, 1583 CE. p. 9

  4. Who founded the Kalachuri Samvat (248 CE)?

    Abhira ruler Ishwarsena. p. 8

  5. To whom does the source attribute the Kollam era (825 CE)?

    Shankaracharya in Malabar — the notes flag this attribution as doubtful. p. 9

Facts Related to Coins

  • First gold coins: Indo-Greek rulers.
  • First pure gold coins: Kushana ruler Vima Kadphises.
  • Maximum number of gold coins: Chandragupta I (as per source).
  • Maximum number of copper coins: Kushana rulers.
  • Lead and tin coins circulated by Satavahana rulers.
  • The Mauryan rulers issued the maximum number of coins.
  • The practice of inscribing writing on coins was first started by the Yavana rulers.
Test your memory

  2. Which rulers circulated lead and tin coins?

    The Satavahanas. p. 9

  3. Which dynasty issued the maximum number of copper coins?

    The Kushanas. p. 9

  4. Who first started inscribing writing on coins?

    The Yavana rulers. p. 9

Chapter recap
  • Periods are defined by writing: none (prehistoric) → undeciphered script (protohistoric) → readable script (historical).
  • Of 18 Puranas only five give royal genealogies; Vishnu–Maurya, Vayu–Gupta, Matsya–Satavahana.
  • Eras run from Vikram Samvat (57 BCE) and Shaka Samvat (78 CE, Kanishka) to Akbar’s Ilahi (1583) and Shivaji’s Rajashaka (1673).
  • Coin records: Indo-Greeks first gold, Vima Kadphises first pure gold, Kushanas most copper, Satavahanas lead/tin.
  • Foreign accounts follow a sequence: Megasthenes (Mauryan) → Fa-Hien (CG II) → Hiuen-Tsang (Harsha) → I-Tsing → Arab writers.

Commonly confused: first gold coins (Indo-Greeks) vs first pure gold coins (Vima Kadphises); Fa-Hien (Chandragupta II) vs Hiuen-Tsang (Harsha); Kathopanishad (Yama–Nachiketa) vs Chandogya (Tat Tvam Asi).

Chapter recap
  • Gupta inscriptions: Prayag & Eran (Samudragupta), Udayagiri (Chandragupta II), Bhitari & Junagadh (Skandagupta).
  • Non-Gupta: Hathigumpha (Kharavela), Junagadh/Girnar (Rudradaman), Nasik (Gautami Balashri), Aihole (Pulakeshin II).
  • Post-Mauryan: Besnagar–Heliodorus, Shinkot–Menander, Nanaghat–Nayanika, Ayodhya–Dhandev.
  • Modern discovery of edict sites ran from Girnar (Tod, 1822) to Kalsi (Forrest, 1860).

Commonly confused: Junagadh — both Rudradaman and Skandagupta; Mandsaur — Kumaragupta I (p. 5) and Yashovarman (p. 7); Prayag (Samudragupta) vs Udayagiri (Chandragupta II).

Chapter recap
  • Neolithic firsts: Mehrgarh – earliest wheat and settled life; Lahuradeva – earliest rice; Burzahom – dog burials.
  • IVC limits: Manda (N), Daimabad (S), Alamgirpur (E), Sutkagendor (W).
  • Excavation order: Harappa 1921 → Mohenjo-daro 1922 → Lothal 1955 → Kalibangan 1961 → Dholavira 1967–68.
  • Lothal = dockyard and bead factories; Dholavira = water management; Kalibangan = ploughed fields.

Commonly confused: Harappa (Ravi, left bank, Sahni) vs Mohenjo-daro (Indus, right bank, Banerjee); Lahuradeva (earliest rice) vs Mehrgarh (earliest wheat).

The Vedic Age

Development of Vedic Literature

Vedic literature developed in four layers, each building on the one before.

SamhitasBrahmanasAranyakasUpanishads
Samhitas
Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda.
Brahmanas
Commentaries on the Samhitas.
Aranyakas
Appendices to the Brahmanas, composed in forests.
Upanishads
Special parts of the Aranyakas; considered sources of Indian philosophy.

Vedas: Branches, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads and Special Facts

VedaBranchesBrahmanasAranyakasUpanishads
RigvedaNot mentionedAitareya, Kaushitaki (Shankhayana)Aitareya, KaushitakiAitareya, Kaushitaki
YajurvedaKrishna Yajurveda (Kathaka, Kapishthala, Maitrayani, Taittiriya); Shukla Yajurveda (Kanva [Vajasaneyi Samhita], Madhyandina)Taittiriya, ShatapathaTaittiriya, Maitrayani, BrihadaranyakaTaittiriya, Katha, Maitrayani, Shvetashvatara, Isha, Brihadaranyaka

Special facts
  • Aitareya Brahmana: Rajasuya sacrifice; description of Satya, Treta, Dwapara and Kali Yuga.
  • Shatapatha Brahmana: Yajnavalkya–Maitreyi dialogue, flood story, story of Videgha Madhava, Pururava–Urvashi legend.
  • Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: “Tamaso Ma Jyotirgamaya”; Yajnavalkya–Gargi dialogue.
  • Kathopanishad: Yama–Nachiketa dialogue.
  • Taittiriya Upanishad: gives women the right to wear the sacred thread.
  • Chandogya Upanishad: the oldest Upanishad; Krishna mentioned for the first time; Satyakama Jabala story; dialogue of Uddalaka Aruni and Shvetaketu; mentions three ashramas — Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha.
  • Mundaka Upanishad: “Satyameva Jayate”.
  • Mandukya: the shortest Upanishad.

Chapter recap
  • Vedic literature develops in layers: Samhitas → Brahmanas (commentaries) → Aranyakas (forest texts) → Upanishads (philosophy).
  • Each Veda has a priest and Upaveda: Rig–Hota–Ayurveda, Yajur–Adhvaryu–Dhanurveda, Sama–Udgata–Gandharvaveda, Atharva–Brahma–Shilpaveda.
  • Rigveda: Gayatri in Mandala 3, Soma Mandala 9, Purusha Sukta (four varnas) in Mandala 10.
  • Aitareya Brahmana names regional polities: Samrajya (E), Swarajya (W), Vairajya (N), Bhojya (S), Rajya (centre).
  • Rivers: Parushni–Ravi, Vitasta–Jhelum, Asikni–Chenab, Shutudri–Sutlej, Vipasha–Beas.

Commonly confused: Chandogya (oldest Upanishad) vs Mandukya (shortest); Shatapatha Brahmana (Yajnavalkya–Maitreyi) vs Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (Yajnavalkya–Gargi); Rajasuya (coronation) vs Ashvamedha (expansion).

Chapter recap
  • Mahavira (Vardhaman), 24th Tirthankara: born 599 BCE Kundagrama, Kaivalya by the Rijupalika, died 527 BCE Pawapuri.
  • Parshvanatha (23rd) gave four vows; Mahavira added Brahmacharya.
  • First council (Pataliputra, Sthulabhadra) compiled 12 Angas and saw the Shvetambara–Digambara split; second (Vallabhi) codified 11.
  • Symbols: Rishabhdev–bull, Neminath–conch, Parshvanath–snake, Mahavira–lion.
  • Kalpasutra – Bhadrabahu (also Chandragupta Maurya’s teacher).

Commonly confused: Syadvada (relativity) vs Anekantavada (multiplicity); Neminath (Urjayant) and Arishtanemi (Girnar) — listed separately but one Tirthankara in the source’s own list.

Eightfold Path and Buddhist Philosophy

The Eightfold Path is the Fourth Noble Truth, “Dukha Nirodhagamini Pratipada”, also called the Middle Path; with eight steps it is called the Ashtangika Marg.

Right View
Understanding the true nature of things.
Right Intention
Thoughts free from greed, hatred, violence.
Right Speech
Avoidance of harsh words.
Right Action
Following righteous deeds.
Right Livelihood
Virtuous livelihood.
Right Effort
Physical/mental health (as per source).
Right Mindfulness
Pious thoughts.
Right Concentration
Meditation and focus.
Buddhist philosophy
Atheism
No belief in divine power.
Momentariness
Nothing in the world is permanent.
Anatma
“Emphasis on self-consciousness” (as per source).
Shunyavada
All worldly objects are devoid of ultimate reality.
Rebirth
Buddhism believes in rebirth.

Chapter recap
  • Buddha: born 563 BCE Lumbini, enlightened at 35 at Gaya, first sermon Sarnath, died 483 BCE Kushinagar.
  • The Eightfold Path is the Fourth Noble Truth (Middle Path).
  • Tripitaka: Vinaya (Upali), Sutta (Ananda), Abhidhamma (Moggaliputta Tissa).
  • Councils: Rajagriha → Vaishali → Pataliputra → Kashmir; patrons Ajatashatru → Kalashoka → Ashoka → Kanishka.
  • Fourth Council produced the final Hinayana–Mahayana division.

Commonly confused: Mahavira (father Siddhartha, wife Yashoda) vs Buddha (childhood name Siddhartha, wife Yashodhara); Purva Mimamsa (Jaimini) vs Uttara Mimamsa (Badarayana); Dvaita (Madhva) vs Dvaitadvaita (Nimbarka).

Chandragupta Maurya, Kautilya and Bindusara

  • Founder of the Maurya dynasty: Chandragupta Maurya; last ruler: Brihadratha.
  • Chandragupta became a disciple of Jain monk Bhadrabahu and died at Shravanabelagola in 298 BCE through Sallekhana.
  • 305 BCE: war between Seleucus (ruler of the eastern part of Alexander’s empire) and Chandragupta.
  • Seleucus sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta’s court; Megasthenes wrote Indica (original not available).
  • Megasthenes’ seven classes of Indian society: Philosophers, Farmers, Pastoralists, Artisans, Warriors, Supervisors, Councillors.
  • Chandragupta’s Prime Minister and Chief Priest: Kautilya (Vishnugupta / Chanakya), author of the Arthashastra.
  • Bindusara asked Antiochus of Syria for three things: sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher.

Kautilya compared the state to a human body with seven organs; he held the king to be the supreme organ and supported monarchy.

Fourteen Major Rock Edicts of Ashoka

  1. Prohibition of animal slaughter.
  2. Medical facilities for humans and animals in Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputra, Keralaputra, Tamraparni, Yavana kingdoms, Antiyoka and their neighbours.
  3. Appointment of three officials: Yukta, Rajjuka, Pradeshika.
  4. Beating of war drums replaced by the “drum of Dhamma”.
  5. In the 13th year of coronation, appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras.
  6. Reporters instructed to inform about the people’s condition.
  7. All sects to live everywhere.
  8. Beginning of Dhamma tours.
  9. Declaring Dhamma as the best welfare.
  10. Emphasis on superiority of the Dhamma policy.
  11. Mention of Dhamma charity.
  12. Emphasis on religious tolerance.
  13. Description of the Kalinga conquest (261 BCE); mentions five Greek kings, Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputra, Keralaputra and Tamraparni.
Source check The source gives contents only for 13 edicts (the last line, about five Greek kings, belongs to the 13th edict); no separate content is given for the 14th.

Chapter recap
  • Of 16 Mahajanapadas, eight lay in present UP (Malla, Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Chedi, Panchala, Shurasena, Kuru).
  • Chandragupta Maurya: Kautilya as minister, Megasthenes at court, died at Shravanabelagola (298 BCE).
  • Ashoka: accession 273 BCE → coronation 269 → Kalinga 261 → Third Council 250 → reign ends 232 BCE.
  • Rock Edicts mainly preach Dhamma; RE 13 alone describes Kalinga and names five Greek kings.
  • Kautilya’s Saptanga: king = head; Mauryan departments had 18 Tirthas.

Commonly confused: Samaharta (revenue collector) vs Sannidhata (treasury head); Dronamukha (800 villages) vs Kharvatika (200); Amitraghata (Bindusara) vs Devanampiya Priyadarshi (Ashoka).

Chapter recap
  • Foreign rulers: Indo-Greek Menander (Sakala), Shaka Nahapana, Parthian Gondophernes, Kushan Kanishka (Purushpur).
  • Kushans: Kujula Kadphises (founder) → Vima Kadphises (Rabatak) → Kanishka (Saka era 78 AD, date conflict flagged).
  • Three Sangams under the Pandyas: Madurai (549 members) → Kapadapuram (59, Tolkappiyam) → Madurai (49, Nakkirar).
  • Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sitalai Sattanar) form a linked pair.

Commonly confused: Kujula Kadphises (founder) vs Vima Kadphises (first pure gold coins); Uraiyur (Chola) vs Madurai (Pandya) vs Vanchi (Chera); Rudradaman placed under Kushans in source though generally a Shaka.

  • Gupta reigns: Chandragupta I (319–335, Gupta Era) → Samudragupta (335–375) → Chandragupta II (375–415).

Texts and Their Authors (Music)

Pundarik Vitthal
Indian musician associated with “Rag Mala”; wrote Sadrag-Chandrodaya on music; composed Ragmanjari at the instruction of Raja Mansingh.
Srikanth
Associated with Rasa Kaumudi (on vocal and instrumental music and dance); student of Pundarik Vitthal; court poet of Satrusalya.
Somnath
Telugu Brahmin of Rajahmundry associated with Raga Vibodh; described ragas in terms of the Janya-Janaka or Thata-Raga system.
Venkatamakhin
Associated with Chaturdandiprakashika; Indian poet and composer of Carnatic music. The work introduced a theoretical melakarta system to classify ragas in Carnatic music.

Chapter recap
  • Harsha (606–647 CE) ruled from Kannauj but was defeated by Pulakeshin II (Aihole inscription; Battle of Narmada 630).
  • Pallavas of Kanchi: Mahendravarman I (monolithic temples), Narasimhavarman I (Badami 642), Rajasimha (Kailashnath, Shore temple).
  • Cholas: Vijayalaya → Rajaraja I (Thanjavur Brihadeeswara) → Rajendra I (Gangaikonda); autonomous villages run by Variyams.
  • Sun temples: Martand (Lalitaditya), Modhera (Bhimdev I), Konark (Narasimhadeva I, Black Pagoda).

Commonly confused: Takkolam (949 CE) victor — Rashtrakutas (p. 16) vs Cholas (p. 17); Kailashnath at Kanchi (Pallava) vs Brihadeeswara at Thanjavur (Chola).

Medieval Indian History

From the Tripartite Struggle and the Turkish invasions through the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and the Bahmani kingdoms, the Bhakti–Sufi movements, the Mughals and the Marathas.

Early Medieval North India and the Turkish Invasions

North India (800–1200 CE) – the Tripartite Struggle

Three powers fought for about a century to control Kannauj, the prize city of North India.

Cause

Duration

Chapter recap
  • The Tripartite Struggle (about 100 years) for Kannauj was won by the Gurjara-Pratiharas.
  • Qasim (712) → Mahmud (17 raids, Somnath 1026) → Ghori (Multan 1175, Tarain 1191/1192, Chandawar 1194).
  • Mahmud’s court scholars: Al-Biruni, Utbi, Firdausi, Baihaqi.
  • Ghori lost to Prithviraj in 1191 but won in 1192.

Commonly confused: First Tarain (1191, Chauhan won) vs Second Tarain (1192, Ghori won); Dantidurga (Rashtrakuta) vs Gopala (Pala) vs Nagabhata I (Pratihara).

Slave Dynasty Rulers

Qutbuddin Aibak and Iltutmish
Qutbuddin Aibak
Established the Slave dynasty in 1206 CE; known as “Lakhbaksh” and “Quran Khan”; died 1210 CE. Constructions: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (Delhi), Adhai Din ka Jhopra (Ajmer); initiated construction of the Qutub Minar (Delhi).
Iltutmish
In 1211 CE shifted capital from Lahore to Delhi; completed the Qutub Minar; introduced the Iqta system; formed the organisation of 40 noble slaves, “Turkan-i-Chahalgani”; issued coins Tanka (silver) and Jital (copper).
Razia and Balban
Razia
Daughter and successor of Iltutmish; the only woman to become Sultan of Delhi; Altunia revolted against her; she married Altunia.
Balban
Real name Bahauddin; abolished “Turkan-i-Chahalgani”; adopted the title “Zille Ilahi” and called himself “Niamat-e-Khudai”; introduced the Iranian customs of “Sijda” and “Paibos”; started celebrating the Nauroz festival; adopted the policy of “Blood and Iron”.

Khilji Dynasty Rulers

Jalaluddin Firuz Khilji (1290–96)
Killed Kayumars and established the Khilji dynasty; Malik Chhajju revolted during his reign; murdered in 1296 CE by his nephew Alauddin.
Alauddin Khilji (1296–1316)
Title “Sikandar Sani” (Second Alexander); first invasion against Gujarat; obtained the slave Malik Kafur from Gujarat.
Last ruler
Nasiruddin Khusro Shah.
Measures of Alauddin Khilji
  • Measured land and collected revenue accordingly; established Diwan-i-Mustakhraj for this purpose.
  • Implemented market control / price control policy.
  • Started branding of horses and recording soldiers’ descriptions.

Tughlaq Dynasty Rulers

Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320–25)
Founder of the Tughlaq dynasty (Ghazi Malik, took the throne in 1320 as Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq); built Tughlaqabad; policy of leniency; first Sultan to construct canals.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–51)
Real name Ulugh Khan (Juna Khan). Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta came in 1333 CE (travelogue Rihla) and was appointed Qazi of Delhi. Established the agriculture department Diwan-i-Amir Kohi.
Last Tughlaq ruler
Nasiruddin Mahmud (1394–1412); Timur invaded Delhi in 1398 during his reign.
Major projects of Muhammad bin Tughlaq
  1. 1325 Increase of taxes in the Doab.
  2. 1326–27 Transfer of capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri).
  3. 1330 Circulation of token currency.
  4. 1332 Khurasan campaign.
  5. 1337 Qarachil (Karachil) campaign.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–88)
  • Born 1309, died 20 September 1388; ruled the Delhi Sultanate 1351–1388.
  • Imposed only the four taxes permitted under Islamic law: Kharaj, Khums, Jizya, Zakat.
  • First to impose Jizya on Brahmins.
  • Issued the coin Shashgani.
  • First Sultan of Delhi to levy an irrigation tax (Haq-i-Sharb).
  • First to establish a Public Works Department.
  • Founded cities: Fatehabad, Hisar, Firozpur, Jaunpur, Firozabad.
  • Established Diwan-i-Khairat, Dar-ul-Shafa, Diwan-i-Bandagaan.
  • Wrote an autobiography, Futuhat-i-Firozshahi.
  • Contributed to architecture in the same way as Shah Jahan did years later.
  • His tomb is in Hauz Khas (New Delhi), near the tank built by Alauddin Khilji.
Remember The Tughlaq dynasty was a Muslim dynasty of Turkic origin.

Lodi Dynasty Rulers

Bahlol Lodi (1451–89)
Founder of the Lodi dynasty; issued the coin Bahlol; conquered Jaunpur and merged it with the Sultanate.
Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517)
Founded Agra in 1504 and made it capital; introduced “Gaj-e-Sikandari” for land measurement; wrote poems under the pen-name “Gulrukhi”; an Ayurvedic text was translated into Persian as Farhang-e-Sikandari; the music treatise Lazzat-e-Sikandari Shahi was composed.
Ibrahim Lodi (1517–26)
Last ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; defeated by Rana Sanga at Khatauli (1518); defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

Chapter recap
  • Dynasties: Slave (1206–1290) → Khilji (1290–1320) → Tughlaq (1320–1414) → Sayyid (1414–1451) → Lodi (1451–1526).
  • Iltutmish consolidated (Delhi capital, Iqta, Chahalgani); Balban centralised (Zille Ilahi, Blood and Iron).
  • Alauddin: market control, Diwan-i-Mustakhraj, branding of horses; campaigns from Devagiri to Dwarasamudra.
  • Tughlaqs: MBT’s experiments (Daulatabad, token currency) vs Firoz’s welfare and taxes; Timur’s invasion 1398.
  • Lodis: Sikandar founded Agra (1504); Ibrahim lost at Panipat (1526).

Commonly confused: Iltutmish (formed Chahalgani) vs Balban (abolished it); Aibak (began Qutub Minar) vs Iltutmish (completed it); Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (Alauddin, revenue) vs Diwan-i-Amir Kohi (MBT, agriculture).

Revenue (Tax) System and the History of Jizya

Ushr
Land tax on Muslims.
Kharaj
Land tax on non-Muslims.
Zakat
Religious tax on Muslims (1/40th of property).
Jizya
Religious tax on non-Muslims.
Jizya tax through the centuries
  1. 712 Muhammad bin Qasim – first to impose Jizya.
  2. 1351 Firoz Shah Tughlaq – first ruler to impose Jizya on Brahmins.
  3. 1564 Akbar – abolished Jizya.
  4. 1674 Aurangzeb – reimposed Jizya.
  5. 1713 Farrukhsiyar – abolished Jizya.
  6. 1717 Farrukhsiyar – reimposed Jizya.
  7. 1719 Muhammad Shah – abolished Jizya.
Source check The 1674 date for Aurangzeb’s reimposition is as given in the source; it is commonly dated 1679.

Chapter recap
  • Department founders: Balban (Arz), Alauddin (Mustakhraj, Riyasat), MBT (Amir Kohi), Firoz (four welfare departments).
  • Taxes: Ushr/Kharaj (land) and Zakat/Jizya (religious), split by Muslim/non-Muslim.
  • Jizya: Qasim (712) → Firoz on Brahmins → Akbar abolished (1564) → Aurangzeb reimposed → Muhammad Shah abolished (1719).
  • Amir Khusro’s works track successive rulers: Bughra Khan/Kaiqubad, Jalaluddin, Alauddin, Mubarak, Ghiyasuddin.

Commonly confused: Mustaufi (auditor) vs Mushrif (accountant); Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence) vs Diwan-i-Rasalat (foreign); Tarikh-e-Firozshahi (Barani) vs Futuhat-e-Firozshahi (Firoz himself).

Vijayanagara: Important Events and Titles

  • First ruler: Harihara I.
  • Title “Ved Marg Pratishthapak” adopted by Bukka I.
  • To commemorate Kumar Kampana’s conquest of Madurai, his wife Gangadevi wrote Madura Vijayam.
  • “Battle of the Goldsmith’s Daughter”: between Devaraya I and Bahmani ruler Firuz Shah.
  • Devaraya II was given the title “Rajbatkar” and was also called “Immadi Devaraya”.
  • Krishnadevaraya: built the Hazara Ramaswamy and Vittal Swami temples; founded the city of Nagalpur; titles “Andhra Bhoja” and “Yavan Raj Sthapanacharya”; authored Amuktamalyada (Telugu) and Jambavati Kalyanam.
  • Battle of Talikota (January 1565): alliance of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara; also called “Rakshasi Tangadi” or “Banni Hatti”; Vijayanagara leader: Rama Raya.
Source check “Rajbatkar” is unclear in source (the title of Devaraya II is often given as Gajabetekara). Source spells “Jamavati Kalyanam”.

Chapter recap
  • Vijayanagara: Sangama (1336) → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu (to 1647).
  • Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva): Andhra Bhoja, Amuktamalyada, Ashtadiggajas, visited by Barbosa and Paes.
  • Bahmani split into Bijapur (1489), Ahmadnagar & Berar (1490), Golconda (1518), Bidar (1527).
  • Talikota (Jan 1565): Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Rama Raya of Vijayanagara.

Commonly confused: Nicolo Conti (Devaraya I) vs Abdur Razzaq (Devaraya II); Nizam Shahi (Ahmadnagar) vs Imad Shahi (Berar); Adil Shahi (Bijapur) vs Qutb Shahi (Golconda).

Bhakti and Sufi Movements and Philosophical Schools

Bhakti Movement

  • In South India, Alvar and Nayanar saints spread Bhakti — Alvars were devotees of Vishnu, Nayanars of Shiva.
  • In Maharashtra a Vaishnava Bhakti tradition existed, divided into the Varkari and Dharakari sects.
  • Varkari sect worshipped Vitthal / Vithoba (a form of Krishna); Dharakari sect worshipped Rama.

Chapter recap
  • Bhakti: Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva) in the south; Varkari (Vitthal) and Dharakari (Rama) in Maharashtra.
  • Acharyas: Shankara (Advaita), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhva (Dvaita), Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabha (Shuddhadvaita).

  1. 21 Apr 1526 First Battle of Panipat – Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi.

  3. 29 Jan 1528 Battle of Chanderi – Babur defeated Medini Rai.
  4. 5/6 May 1529 Battle of Ghaghra – Babur defeated Mahmud Lodi.
  5. 26 Dec 1530 Death of Babur.

Humayun (1530–1556) and Sher Shah Suri (1540–1545)

  • Humayun: born 1508 in Kabul; ascended throne 1530 at Agra; died 1556. Humayun-nama written by Gulbadan Begum.
  1. 1532 Battle of Dauraha / Dewra (Dauharia), on the Gomti – Humayun defeated Afghan Mahmud Lodi (p. 22: the combined forces of Mahmud Lodi and Sher Shah).
  2. 26 Jun 1539 Battle of Chausa (Buxar, Bihar) – Sher Shah won; Humayun nearly lost his life and was saved by a water-carrier (bhisti) named Nizam; Sher Khan took the title “Sher Shah” after this victory.
  3. 17 May 1540 Battle of Kannauj / Bilgram – Humayun’s decisive defeat; Sher Shah captured Delhi.
  4. 15 May 1555 Battle of Machhiwara – Humayun defeated Sikandar Sur.
  5. 22 Jun 1555 Battle of Sirhind – Humayun defeated Sikandar Sur again.
  6. Jul 1555 Humayun recaptured Delhi.
Source check p. 22 reads “Humayun’s life was lost in this battle named Nizam. Bhisti saved him” — garbled; read as above.
Sher Shah Suri
  • Childhood name: Farid Khan; Muhammad Bahar Khan Lohani gave him the title “Sher Khan”.
  • Sat on the throne of Delhi in 1540; died in 1545 during the victory at Kalinjar.
  • Introduced the Kabuliat and Patta system.

Major works of Akbar
  1. 1562 Abolished slavery; freed himself from “Haramdal” (harem party / petticoat government).

  3. 1564 Abolished Jizya.

  9. 1582 Closed the Ibadat Khana; declared Din-i-Ilahi.

Jahangir (1605–1627) and Shah Jahan (1628–1657)

Jahangir
Real name Salim; parents Harkha Bai and Akbar; wives Man Bai, Jagat Gosain, Mehrunnisa (Nur Jahan); sons Khusro, Parvez, Shahryar, Jahandar; autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri; tomb at Shahdara; foreign visitors Hawkins, Sir Thomas Roe, Francisco Pelsaert; introduced the Do-aspa and Sih-aspa system; reign called the “Golden Age of Painting”.
Shah Jahan
Real name Khurram; parents Jagat Gosain and Jahangir; wife Arjumand Bano Begum (Mumtaz Mahal); sons Dara Shikoh, Aurangzeb, Murad, Shah Shuja; in 1638 shifted capital from Agra to Delhi; conferred the title “Shahbuland Iqbal” on Dara Shikoh; reign called the “Golden Age of Architecture”; died January 1666; tomb at Agra (in the Taj Mahal).
Dara Shikoh
Translated the Upanishads into Persian as Sirr-e-Akbar.

Chapter recap
  • Babur won at Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi and Ghaghra (1526–29).
  • Humayun lost to Sher Shah (Chausa 1539, Kannauj 1540) and returned in 1555.
  • Akbar: Second Panipat (1556), Jizya abolished (1564), Fatehpur Sikri (1571), Din-i-Ilahi (1582).
  • Jahangir = painting; Shah Jahan = architecture; Aurangzeb won the 1658–59 war of succession.
  • Mughal tiers: Suba → Sarkar → Pargana → Village.

Commonly confused: Moti Masjid at Agra (Shah Jahan) vs Moti Masjid in Red Fort, Delhi (Aurangzeb); Humayun-nama (Gulbadan) vs Qanun-i-Humayuni (Khwandamir); Faujdar (Sarkar head) vs Shiqdar (Pargana head).

Some Important Facts: Bengal Nawabs, Plassey and Buxar

  1. 1717 Farrukhsiyar made Murshid Quli Khan governor of Bengal; he shifted the capital from Dhaka to Murshidabad.
  2. 1740 Alivardi Khan became Nawab after killing Sarfaraz in the Battle of Giria.
  3. 1756 Siraj-ud-Daula became Nawab of Bengal.
  4. 20 Jun 1756 Black Hole (Kala Kothri) incident.
  5. 23 Jun 1757 Battle of Plassey – Siraj-ud-Daula vs Robert Clive.
  6. 1757 / 1760 The British made first Mir Jafar, then (1760) Mir Qasim the puppet Nawab; Mir Qasim shifted the capital from Murshidabad to Munger.
  7. 22 Oct 1764 Battle of Buxar – Mir Qasim, Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh vs English general Hector Munro (Mir Qasim was troubled by the excessive plunder of Bengal).
  8. 12 Aug 1765 First Treaty of Allahabad – Robert Clive and Shah Alam II.
  9. 16 Aug 1765 Second Treaty of Allahabad – Robert Clive and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.
  10. 1765–1772 Dual government (dual rule) in Bengal.

Chapter recap
  • Shivaji: Afzal Khan (1659) → Surat (1664) → Purandar (1665) → escape from Agra (1666) → coronation (1674).
  • Ashtapradhan: Peshwa (PM), Amatya (finance), Sumant (foreign), Senapati (military), Nyayadhish (justice).
  • Anglo-Maratha wars: 1775–82 (Salbai), 1803–05 (after Bassein 1802), 1817–18.
  • Bengal: Plassey (1757) → Mir Jafar → Mir Qasim → Buxar (1764) → Allahabad (1765) → dual government (1765–72).

Commonly confused: Sumant (foreign) vs Sachiv (correspondence); First Treaty of Allahabad (with Shah Alam II) vs Second (with Shuja-ud-Daula); Treaty of Purandar 1665 (Shivaji–Jai Singh) vs Second Purandar 1776 (Peshwa–English).

Lahore1846Governor-General Henry Hardinge and the Lahore Durbar (young Maharaja Dalip Singh); ended the First Anglo-Sikh War.
Amritsar1846The East India Company sold Kashmir to Maharaja Gulab Singh; his descendants ruled until 1947, when Maharaja Hari Singh acceded to India.

Anglo-Maratha Wars

First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82)
  • Cause: Peshwa succession struggle — Raghunath Rao (Raghoba) sought British help to become Peshwa.
  • Parties: Raghunath Rao, Nana Phadnavis and Warren Hastings.
  • Treaty of Purandar (1776): between Nana Phadnavis / Poona Durbar and the Calcutta Government of the English; opposed by the Bombay Government.
  • Treaty of Baragaon (Wadgaon), 1779.
  • Treaty of Salbai (1782): between the English and the Poona Durbar; brought peace for two decades — the British abandoned Raghunath Rao and the Marathas allowed the British peaceful trade.
Second (1803–1805) and Third (1816–1819) Anglo-Maratha Wars
  • Treaty of Bassein (1802): Peshwa Bajirao II and the English.
  • Second war: successful British campaign led by Arthur Wellesley in the Deccan and General Lake in North India. Treaties: Deogaon (1803, Bhonsle), Surji-Arjungaon (1803, Scindia), Rajpur Ghat (1805, Holkar).
  • Third war: started by Hastings’ action against the Pindaris. Treaties: Nagpur (1816, Bhonsle), Gwalior (1817, Scindia), Poona (1817, Bajirao II).

Anglo-Sikh Wars and Maharaja Dalip Singh

WarKey facts
First (1845–1846)Governor-General Lord Hardinge; commander Hugh Gough; Battle of Sobraon (February 1846); Treaty of Lahore (March 1846) – territory south of the Sutlej went to the English; Treaty of Bhairowal (1846) – British troops stationed in Lahore until Raja Dalip Singh came of age.
Second (1848–1849)Battle of Ramnagar (November 1848); Battle of Chillianwala (January 1849); Battle of Gujarat (February 1849) – Sikh forces defeated “under Charles Napier” (as per source); Punjab annexed in March 1849 (29 March 1849, under Dalhousie).
Maharaja Dalip Singh (1843–1849)
  • Minor ruler; protector (regent): Maharani Jind Kaur.
  • Battle of Chillianwala (1849) – Lord Dalhousie; First and Second Anglo-Sikh Wars.
  • 1849: to rule Punjab, Dalhousie formed a council of three, with Sir Henry Lawrence as President.
  • Given an annual pension of 50,000 pounds; converted to Christianity; gave the Kohinoor diamond to the British.
  • Died in France; funeral in England.
Source check Source reads “He died in France Story Funeral in England” – garbled. Battle of Gujarat (1849) is credited to “Charles Napier” in source; the British commander there is usually given as Hugh Gough.

Chapter recap
  • Companies: Portuguese 1505, English 1600, Dutch 1602, Danish 1616, French 1664.
  • Carnatic wars ended French ambitions (Wandiwash 1760); Plassey (1757) laid the foundation and Buxar (1764) established real power.
  • Mysore: four wars, ending with Tipu’s death (4 May 1799).
  • Marathas: Salbai (1782) → Bassein (1802) → Pindari campaign and the 1817–18 treaties.
  • Sikhs: Lahore/Bhairowal (1846), then annexation of Punjab (29 March 1849).

Commonly confused: Treaty of Purandar 1665 (Jai Singh–Shivaji) vs Purandar 1776 (British–Marathas); Treaty of Lahore (ended Sikh war) vs Treaty of Amritsar (Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh); Madras 1769 (Mysore I) vs Mangalore (Mysore II).

Governors-General, Viceroys, Commissions and Land Revenue

Acts and Facts Related to the Governor-General / Viceroy

Governor-General of Bengal (1773)Governor-General of India (1833)Viceroy of India (1858)Post abolished (1948)
  • Regulating Act, 1773: the Governor of Bengal became Governor-General of Bengal — Warren Hastings.
  • Charter Act, 1833: Governor-General of Bengal made Governor-General of India — Lord William Bentinck (last GG of Bengal, first GG of India).
  • Government of India Act, 1858: Governor-General became Viceroy of India — Lord Canning (last GG and first Viceroy).
  • The post of Viceroy was abolished in 1948; Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy (and first Governor-General of independent India).
  • C. Rajagopalachari (1948–1950): last Governor-General of India and the first Indian Governor-General of independent India.

Governors-General and Their Events (1773–1856)

Governor-GeneralEvents / facts
Warren Hastings (1773–1785)First Governor-General of Bengal; Regulating Act 1773; Pitt’s India Act 1784; Rohilla War (1774); Ring Fence policy; Supreme Court at Calcutta; First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82); Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84); Treaty of Salbai (1782); first Madrasa in Calcutta (1781); “Father of Judicial Service in India”.
Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793)Third Mysore War (1790–92); Treaty of Srirangapatnam (1792); Cornwallis Code (1793); Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793); “Father of Civil Services and Police Services in India”; died 5 October 1805 at Ghazipur (U.P.), where his tomb is.
Lord Wellesley (1798–1805)Subsidiary Alliance (1798); Fourth Mysore War (1799); Treaty of Bassein (1802); Second Maratha War (1803–05); Fort William College, Calcutta (1801); Infanticide prohibition.
Lord Hastings (1813–1823)Anglo-Nepal War (1814–16); Treaty of Sugauli (1816); Third Maratha War (1817–19), after which the policy of non-intervention ended; disintegration of the Maratha Confederacy; Peshwa post abolished (1818); Ryotwari system (1820, Bombay and Madras, by Thomas Munro); Mahalwari system in Awadh and North-Western Provinces.
Lord William Bentinck (1828–1835)Last GG of Bengal and first GG of India (Charter Act 1833); abolition of Sati by regulation (1829); suppression of Thugi with Colonel Sleeman (1830); Calcutta Medical College (1835).
Charles Metcalfe“Liberator of the Press”.
Lord AucklandFirst Anglo-Afghan War (1839–1842); Hindu Women’s Property Act (1837).
Lord Ellenborough (1842–44)First Anglo-Afghan War ended; Sindh annexed (1843); abolition of slavery (Act V of 1843).
Lord HardingeFirst Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46).
Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856)Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–49), Punjab annexed 29 March 1849; occupation of Lower Burma (1852); Doctrine of Lapse; Kohinoor sent to Queen Victoria; Wood’s Despatch (1854); first railway Bombay–Thane (34 km, 1853), second line Calcutta–Raniganj (1854); first Public Works Department; “Father of Railways and Telegraph”.

  1. 1848 Satara
  2. 1849 Jaitpur, Sambalpur
  3. 1850 Baghat
  4. 1852 Udaipur
  5. 1853 Jhansi
  6. 1854 Nagpur
  7. 1856 Awadh (on charges of misrule)

Viceroys and Their Events (1856–1948)

ViceroyEvents / facts
Lord Canning (1856–58 & 1858–62)Last GG of India and first Viceroy; Revolt of 1857; universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857); end of Company rule (Government of India Act 1858); Mughal emperor’s title abolished; Indian Councils Act 1861; Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (1856).
Lord John Lawrence (1864–1869)Bhutan War (1865); High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1865); severe famine in Odisha, Rajputana, Bundelkhand; Famine Commission; telegraph lines between Europe and India; Punjab Tenancy Act.
Lord Mayo (1869–1872)Archaeological Survey Department (1871); High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1865 — listed under Mayo on p. 49); first Census of India (1872); Mayo College, Ajmer (1875).
Lord NorthbrookNative Marriage Act (1872).
Lord Lytton (1876–1880)Vernacular Press Act 1878 (called “thunderbolt from the sky” by Surendranath Banerjee); Arms Act 1878; Second Afghan War (1878–80); Queen Victoria took the title “Kaiser-e-Hind”; first Famine Commission (1878) under Richard Strachey; Statutory Civil Service (1878); ICS age limit reduced from 21 to 19.
Lord Ripon (1880–84)Regular census began (1881); Local Self-Government resolution (1882) — “Father of Local Self-Government”; Education Commission under William Hunter (1882) for primary education; Vernacular Press Act repealed (1882); Ilbert Bill controversy (1883) — allowing Indian judges to try Europeans, called the “White Mutiny”.
Lord Dufferin (1884–86)Indian National Congress founded (1885) by A.O. Hume; Allahabad University established (1887) during his tenure.
Lord LansdowneAge of Consent Act (1891).
Lord Curzon (1899–1905)Commissions: Famine 1900 (Antony MacDonnell), Irrigation 1901 (Colin Scott Moncrieff), Railway 1901 (Thomas Robertson), Police 1902 (Andrew Fraser), University 1902 (Thomas Raleigh). Partition of Bengal announced at Shimla on 19 July 1905, approved September 1905.
Lord Minto II (1905–1910)Congress split at Surat (1907); Morley-Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Lord Hardinge II (1910–1916)Partition of Bengal annulled at the Delhi Durbar and capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi (1911); Delhi became capital in 1912; bomb attack on Hardinge in Delhi, 23 December 1912 (Bhai Bal Mukund sentenced to death).
Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921)Reforms of 20 August 1917 (Montagu Declaration) known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
Lord Reading (1921–1926)Only Jewish Viceroy; first ICS exam held simultaneously in London and Allahabad (1922); Public Service Commission established 1 October 1926.
Lord Irwin (1926–1931)Hartog-Butler Committee (1927) on princely states; Simon Commission arrived 3 February 1928; Civil Disobedience Movement; First Round Table Conference; Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931); Sharda Act.
Lord WillingdonCommunal Award, Poona Pact.
Lord Linlithgow (1936–1944)First provincial (general) elections 1936–37 — Congress formed governments in 8 of 11 provinces; Individual Satyagraha; Cripps Mission (1942), called a “post-dated cheque” by Gandhi; Quit India Movement launched 8 August 1942 with the slogan “Do or Die”.
Lord Wavell (1944–1947)C.R. Formula; Sargent Plan on education (1944); Wavell Plan (1945); Shimla Conference; Cabinet Mission; on 20 February 1947 PM Clement Attlee declared transfer of power by June 1948.
Lord Mountbatten (1947–1948)Last Governor-General and Viceroy of British India; became first Governor-General of independent India; Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947 (partition); Indian Independence Act.
Source check Source (p. 39) spells “Lord Wellington” and “Lord Bevel”; these mean Lord Willingdon and Lord Wavell. p. 39 calls Bentinck “First Governor General of British India”.

Chapter recap
  • Title changes: GG of Bengal (1773, Hastings) → GG of India (1833, Bentinck) → Viceroy (1858, Canning) → abolished 1948.
  • Cornwallis: Permanent Settlement 1793; Wellesley: Subsidiary Alliance; Dalhousie: Doctrine of Lapse and railways.
  • Lytton’s Vernacular Press Act (1878) was repealed by Ripon (1882).
  • Curzon’s commissions: famine, irrigation, railway, police, university; Bengal partition 1905, annulled 1911.
  • Land revenue: Zamindari 19%, Ryotwari 51%, Mahalwari 30%.

Commonly confused: Hunter Commission 1882 (education) vs Hunter Committee 1919 (Punjab); Raleigh 1902 (universities) vs Sadler 1917 (Calcutta University); Ryotwari (farmer pays) vs Mahalwari (headman pays).

The Revolt of 1857

Outbreak of the Revolt of 1857

  • 29 March 1857: Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry at Barrackpore (Parganas, West Bengal) shot his Sergeant Major Hewson and revolted; he was hanged on 8 April 1857.
  • The revolt began on 10 May 1857 at Meerut.
  • Governor-General of India: Lord Canning; Mughal ruler: Bahadur Shah II ‘Zafar’.

Socio-Religious Reform, Social Legislation and the Press

Raja Rammohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj

  • Born 22 May 1772 at Radhanagar, Hooghly (Bengal); died 27 September 1833.
  • Title “Raja” given by Mughal Emperor Akbar II.
  • Also called: ‘Yugdoot’ (by Subhash Chandra Bose), ‘Father of Constitutional Movement’ (by Surendranath Banerjee), ‘Herald of Indian Renaissance’, ‘Father of Modern India’, ‘Father of Indian Nationalism’, ‘Morning Star of Indian Renaissance’, ‘Bridge between Past and Future’, ‘Messiah of New India’, ‘First Modern Man’, ‘Yug Purush’, etc.
  • Newspapers: Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali, 1821); Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian, 1822).
  1. 1809 Wrote Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin (Gift to Monotheists).
  2. 1815 Founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815–17, Calcutta).
  3. 1817 Hindu College (David Hare College) with David Hare; Calcutta College.
  4. 1820 Wrote Precepts of Jesus.
  5. 1825 Vedanta College.
  6. 1828 Brahmo Sabha (Brahmo Samaj), Calcutta.
  7. 1829 Abolition of Sati with Lord William Bentinck.

Swami Dayanand Saraswati and Swami Vivekananda

Swami Dayanand Saraswati and the Arya Samaj
  • Born 12 February 1824, Tankara (Gujarat); childhood name Mool Shankar.
  • Founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, Bombay.
  • Slogans: “Back to the Vedas”, “India is for Indians”; first to use the term “Swaraj”.
  • Called the “Martin Luther of India”.
  • Reform work: revival of the Vedas, opposition to social-religious evils, Shuddhi Movement, cow protection movement.
  • Books: Satyarth Prakash (1874, Sanskrit) — “Bible of the Arya Samaj”; Pakhanda Khandan (1866); Criticism of Advaita (1873).
  • First person to accept Hindi as the national language; said “Even the worst native rule is better than the best foreign rule”.
Swami Vivekananda and the Ramakrishna Mission
  • Born 12 January 1863, Calcutta; childhood name Narendra Nath Dutta; father Vishwanath Dutta.
  • Guru: Ramakrishna Paramhansa.
  • Founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 at Belur (Calcutta).

Chapter recap
  • Rammohan Roy: Atmiya Sabha (1815) → Brahmo Sabha (1828) → Sati abolition with Bentinck (1829).
  • Dayanand: Arya Samaj (1875, Bombay), ‘Back to the Vedas’; Vivekananda: Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Belur).
  • Reformers drove Acts: Vidyasagar (widow remarriage 1856), Keshav Chandra Sen (1872), Malabari (Age of Consent 1891).
  • First papers: Bengal Gazette 1780 (English), Samachar Darpan 1818 (Bengali), Udant Martand 1826 (Hindi).
  • Sikh Gurus: Angad (Gurmukhi), Arjun Dev (Granth), Hargobind (Akal Takht), Gobind Singh (Khalsa).

Commonly confused: Brahmo Samaj (1828, Rammohan) vs Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang/Ranade) vs Arya Samaj (1875, Dayanand); Satyashodhak Samaj (Phule) vs Bahujan Samaj (Mukundrao Patil); Mirat-ul-Akhbar (Persian) vs Jam-e-Jahan-Numa (Urdu).

Muslim League, the Surat Split and Bal Gangadhar Tilak

Formation of the Muslim League (1906)
  • December 1906: at the invitation of Nawab Salimullah Khan of Dhaka, the ‘All India Muslim Educational Conference’ was held in Dhaka, where Salimullah proposed an All India Muslim League.
  • The League was formed in 1906 with its headquarters at Lucknow; Aga Khan was its first President.
Surat Session of 1907
  • Presided over by Ras Bihari Ghosh; Congress split into Moderates and Extremists.
  • Reason: differences on the methods of conducting the Swadeshi Movement.
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
  • Titles: “Lokmanya”, “Uncrowned King of India”; Valentine Chirol (author of Indian Unrest) called him “Father of Indian Unrest”.
  • Newspapers: Maratha, Kesari (1881). Started the Ganapati Festival (1893) and Shivaji Festival (1895).
  • 1908: charged with sedition for writings in Kesari; sentenced to 6 years in Mandalay Jail (Burma), where he wrote Gita Rahasya.
  • Criticised the Congress for its politics of prayer, petition and protest.

First Phase of the Revolutionary Movement

  • “Mitra Mela”, founded by V.D. Savarkar in 1899, became the secret society “Abhinav Bharat” in 1904.
  • P. Mitra established the Anushilan Samiti in Bengal.
  • 30 April 1908: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw a bomb at judge Kingsford’s carriage in Muzaffarpur; Kingsford survived. Prafulla Chaki killed himself; Khudiram was arrested and hanged in 1908 “at the age of just 15” (as per source).
  • 23 December 1912: bomb thrown at Viceroy Lord Hardinge II’s procession in Delhi; Ras Bihari Bose and Sachin Sanyal played key roles.
Source check Khudiram Bose’s age at execution (15) is as in source; he is usually recorded as 18.

Chapter recap
  • Pre-Congress associations: Landholders’ Society (1838) → Indian Association (1876) → Bombay Presidency Association (1885).
  • Congress 1885 (Bombay, Bonnerjee) → Surat split 1907 → Lucknow Pact 1916 → Poorna Swaraj 1929.

The Gandhian Era and Mass Movements

Chronology of Major Events of the Freedom Movement

  1. 7 Aug 1905 Swadeshi Movement.
  2. 16 Aug 1905 Mourning Day against the Partition of Bengal.
  3. 30 Dec 1906 Formation of the Muslim League.
  4. 1907 Madam Cama hoists the first Indian flag in Germany; split of Congress (Surat session).
  5. 1908 Branch of the Muslim League in London.
  6. 12 Dec 1911 Delhi Durbar.
  7. 1 Nov 1913 Formation of the Ghadar Party.
  8. 1914 Komagata Maru incident.
  9. 9 Jan 1915 Gandhi arrives in India; awarded “Kaiser-i-Hind” (1915).
  10. Apr 1916 Tilak establishes the Home Rule League at Poona.
  11. Sep 1916 Annie Besant establishes the Home Rule League.
  12. Dec 1916 Lucknow Pact.
  13. 10 Apr 1917 Champaran Satyagraha.
  14. 20 Aug 1917 Montagu Declaration.
  15. Feb–Mar 1918 Ahmedabad Mill Strike.
  16. Mar 1918 Kheda Satyagraha.
  17. Mar 1919 Rowlatt Act.
  18. 13 Apr 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
  19. Sep 1919 Khilafat Committee formed; Khilafat Conference (November 1919).
  20. 1 Aug 1920 Start of Non-Cooperation Movement; death of Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
  21. Sep 1920 Special Calcutta session.
  22. Dec 1920 Nagpur session passes the Non-Cooperation resolution.
  23. 4–5 Feb 1922 Chauri Chaura incident.
  24. 12 Feb 1922 Non-Cooperation suspended.
  25. 10 Mar 1922 Arrest of Gandhi.
  26. 1922–23 Peshawar Conspiracy Case.
  27. Jan 1923 Swaraj Party formed.
  28. 1924 Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case; Hindustan Republican Association formed; Gandhi–C.R. Das Pact (November).
  29. 9 Aug 1925 Kakori Train Action.
  30. 1925 Vithalbhai Patel becomes President (of the Central Legislative Assembly).
  31. 3 Feb 1928 Simon Commission arrives in India.
  32. 1928 HSRA formed; Nehru Report (August); Bardoli Satyagraha (October); Saunders assassination (17 December).
  33. 8 Apr 1929 Assembly Bomb Case; Lahore Conspiracy Case (1929).
  34. 12 Mar 1930 Dandi March begins; Civil Disobedience Movement (6 April 1930).
  35. 1930–31 First Round Table Conference.
  36. 5 Mar 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
  37. 23 Mar 1931 Hanging of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev.
  38. Sep–Dec 1931 Second Round Table Conference.
  39. 16 Aug 1932 Communal Award.
  40. 24 Sep 1932 Poona Pact.
  41. Nov–Dec 1932 Third Round Table Conference.
  42. 1934 Congress Socialist Party formed.
  43. May 1939 Forward Bloc formed.
  44. 22 Dec 1939 Muslim League observes Deliverance Day.
  45. Mar 1940 Lahore Resolution for Pakistan.
  46. 8 Aug 1940 August Offer.
  47. Mar 1942 Cripps Mission.
  48. 9 Aug 1942 Quit India Movement.
  49. 1945 Shimla Conference.
  50. 1946 Naval Mutiny.

Jallianwala Bagh, Non-Cooperation and Chauri Chaura

Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919)
  1. 18 Mar 1919 Rowlatt Act passed.
  2. 9 Apr 1919 Punjab leaders Dr. Satyapal and Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew arrested on the order of Lieutenant-Governor Michael O’Dwyer, angering the people.
  3. 10 Apr 1919 Amritsar’s administration handed over to Brigadier-General R. Dyer.
  4. 13 Apr 1919 Baisakhi meeting at Jallianwala Bagh; General Dyer ordered indiscriminate firing.
  • In protest, Shankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy’s Executive Council and Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood.
  • Congress formed an inquiry committee under Madan Mohan Malaviya.
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22)
  • September 1920: special Congress session at Calcutta under Lala Lajpat Rai approved launching Non-Cooperation to attain Swaraj.
  • Gandhi launched the movement on 1 August 1920 — the same day Tilak died.
  • December 1920: the Nagpur annual session finally passed the resolution, presented by C.R. Das.
  • 1921: the “Tilak Swaraj Fund” was set up to run the movement.
  • Gandhi renounced “Kaiser-i-Hind”; Jamnalal Bajaj renounced “Rai Bahadur”.
  • Tagore called the burning of foreign clothes a “cruel waste”.
Chauri Chaura Incident (4 February 1922)
  • At Chauri Chaura, Gorakhpur district, United Provinces.
  • After police fired on a farmers’ procession, an enraged mob set fire to the police station, killing 22 policemen.
  • Result: on 12 February 1922 Gandhi suspended the Non-Cooperation Movement.

    Gorakhpur; Gandhi suspended the movement on 12 Feb 1922. p. 58

Formation of the Swaraj Party (March 1923)

  • Formed by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru at Allahabad in March 1923 to contest the 1923 legislative council elections.
  • C.R. Das president; Motilal Nehru general secretary.
  • In 1925 the party got Vitthalbhai Patel elected President of the Central Legislative Assembly.
Common confusion The chronology on p. 55 dates the Swaraj Party to January 1923; p. 58 says March 1923.

Second Phase of the Revolutionary Movement

  • HRA: formed in October 1924 at Kanpur by Sachindra Sanyal, Ramprasad Bismil, Yogesh Chatterjee and others.
  • Kakori incident (9 August 1925): HRA revolutionaries looted the 8 Down train at Kakori near Lucknow; 29 were arrested and tried. Ramprasad Bismil, Rajendra Lahiri, Roshan Lal and Ashfaqulla were hanged at Gorakhpur, Gonda, Naini and Faizabad respectively; Chandrashekhar Azad escaped.
  • HSRA: in 1928, under Chandrashekhar Azad, the HRA was renamed HSRA at Feroz Shah Kotla grounds, Delhi. Founding members: Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Bhagwati Charan Vohra, Shiv Verma, Jaidev Kapoor, Vijay Kumar Sinha.
  • 17 December 1928: Bhagat Singh, Azad and Rajguru killed Saunders in Lahore to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai’s death.
  • 8 April 1929: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly.
  • Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev were tried in the Lahore Conspiracy Case and executed on 23 March 1931.
  • Chandrashekhar Azad shot himself during a police encounter at Alfred Park, Allahabad, 27 February 1931.
  • 18 April 1930: under Surya Sen (Master Da), the Chittagong branch of the Indian Republican Army attacked the Chittagong Armoury.

Civil Disobedience, Round Table Conferences and the Poona Pact

Civil Disobedience Movement and Dandi March
  • Started with the Dandi March, 12 March 1930: Gandhi marched from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 supporters.
  • After 24 days reached Dandi (Navsari district) on 5 April; broke the salt law on 6 April; covered 390 km in all.
  • American journalist Webb Miller accompanied Gandhi.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact
  • Signed on 5 March 1931 after long discussions; also called the Delhi Pact. As a result Congress agreed to attend the Second RTC.
Round Table Conferences
RTCDatesKey facts
First12 Nov 1930 – Jan 1931Held to discuss the Simon Commission recommendations; failed as Congress did not participate.
Second7 Sep – 1 Dec 1931Gandhi attended as the sole Congress representative (left on 29 Aug 1931 aboard S.S. Rajputana) during Viceroy Lord Willingdon’s time; failed over the demand for separate electorates for Dalits. Associates: Mahadev Desai, Madan Mohan Malaviya, Devdas Gandhi, G.D. Birla, Miraben, Annie Besant, Sarojini Naidu.
Third17 Nov – 24 Dec 1932Congress boycotted; Government of India Bill presented afterwards; Government of India Act passed in 1935.
Remember Dr. B.R. Ambedkar attended all three RTCs; Congress attended only the Second. British PM: Ramsay MacDonald; Viceroy: Lord Willingdon. Muslim representatives demanded separate electorates.
Communal Award and Poona Pact
  1. 16 Aug 1932 PM Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award — Dalits treated as minorities along with Muslims and Sikhs.
  2. 20 Sep 1932 Gandhi began a protest fast in Yerwada Jail.
  3. 24 Sep 1932 Poona Pact: compromise between Ambedkar and Gandhi’s representatives (M.M. Malaviya, Rajendra Prasad, C. Rajagopalachari); draft by Rajagopalachari; signed by Ambedkar and Malaviya.

Major Peasant (Farmers’) Movements

MovementAreaLeadersAgainst / cause
Mapilla (Moplah) Rebellion (1836–1854; 1921–22)Malabar, KeralaK.N. Das, Syed Qazi, Ali MusaliarAtrocities of landlords and British policies (Khilafat issue); Muslim Moplah peasants exploited in land and tax system
PagalpanthiNorthern BengalKaram Shah and TipuLandlords’ atrocities; religious order
Faraizi Movement (1838)Faridpur, BengalHaji Shariatullah and Dadu MiyanReligious reform

Pabna Revolt (1873–76)BengalIshan Chandra Roy, Keshav Chandra Roy, Shambhunath PalLand grabbing, eviction, rent hike
Deccan Revolt (1874–75)Poona, Ahmednagar, Sholapur, SataraBaba Saheb DeshmukhRent hikes on cotton cultivators; eviction by moneylenders
Bijolia Movement (1905, 1913, 1916, 1927)RajasthanSitaram Das, Manik Lal VermaMultiple taxes on peasants
Champaran Satyagraha (1917)Champaran, Motihari, Bettiah, Madhubani (Bihar)Mahatma Gandhi, Rajendra Prasad, Rajkumar Shukla, etc.Tinkathia system – forced indigo cultivation on part of the land
Kheda Satyagraha (1918)Kheda (Gujarat)Mahatma Gandhi, Sardar Vallabhbhai PatelRevenue collection despite crop failure / famine
Awadh Peasant Movement (1920)Pratapgarh, Raebareli, Sultanpur, Faizabad (U.P.)RamchandraIllegal rent collection and eviction
Eka Movement (1921–22)Barabanki, Sitapur, Hardoi, BahraichMadari PasiRent hike
Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)Bardoli taluka, Surat (Gujarat)Vallabhbhai Patel22% increase in land tax (lagaan)
Tebhaga Movement (1946–47)Bengal“Komparam”, Bhuvan SinghSharecroppers to give only one-third (33%) of the crop instead of half
Outcomes of key movements
  • Champaran (1917): Gandhi raised the farmers’ demands; the British abolished the Tinkathia system — Gandhi’s first successful Satyagraha in India.
  • Kheda (1918): the government suspended tax collection and the farmers got relief.
  • Bardoli (1928): farmers refused to pay; the government withdrew the increase; Patel got the title “Sardar”.
  • Tebhaga (1946–47): widely successful; led to reforms in Bengal’s land law and improved the condition of tenant farmers.
  • Moplah (1921): turned into a religious and social conflict with many deaths; not successful, but important in peasant history.
Remember After independence the Bhoodan Movement was led by Vinoba Bhave.

Major tribal revolts in detail
RevoltAreaLeaderCause and result
Bhil Revolt (1818–1831)Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya PradeshGovind Guru (as per source)British forest and tax policies; exploitation by landlords and moneylenders. Suppressed after years of struggle, but inspired protection of tribal rights.
Ho Revolt (1820–1827)Chhota Nagpur (now Jharkhand)—British colonialism and exploitation by landlords (the region was earlier under the Mughals, then the Marathas; worsened under the British). Harshly suppressed, but inspired further tribal movements.
Kol Rebellion (1831–1832)Chhota Nagpur, JharkhandBudhu Bhagat and companionsLoss of land to outsiders and the British tax system; atrocities by outsider landlords. Suppressed, but convinced the British that outside interference caused tribal discontent.
Santhal Rebellion (1855–1856)Santhal Pargana (Bihar and West Bengal)Sido and Kanhu MurmuExcessive taxes, landlord exploitation, moneylenders’ tyranny. Violently resisted but suppressed; led to the creation of the Santhal Pargana.

Chapter recap
  • Gandhi’s early satyagrahas: Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad (1918), Kheda (1918).
  • Rowlatt Act → Jallianwala (13 Apr 1919) → NCM (1 Aug 1920) → Chauri Chaura → suspension (12 Feb 1922).
  • Swaraj Party (1923) worked inside councils; HRA → Kakori (1925) → HSRA (1928) worked outside.
  • Dandi (12 Mar 1930) → Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 Mar 1931) → Second RTC → Communal Award → Poona Pact (24 Sep 1932).
  • Peasant and tribal revolts ran from the Sanyasi rebellion (1763) to Tebhaga (1946–47).

Commonly confused: Communal Award (MacDonald, 16 Aug 1932) vs Poona Pact (24 Sep 1932); Kheda (crop failure) vs Bardoli (tax hike); Eka Movement (Madari Pasi) vs Awadh movement (Ramchandra).

Towards Independence and Partition (1940–1947)

Major Sequence of Events, 1940–1947

  1. 23 Mar 1940 Pakistan Day.
  2. Mar 1942 Cripps Mission.
  3. 8 Aug 1942 Quit India Movement.
  4. Sep 1942 Azad Hind Fauj.
  5. Mar 1944 C. Rajagopalachari Formula.
  6. 14 Jun 1945 Wavell Plan.
  7. 25 Jun – 14 Jul 1945 Shimla Conference.
  8. Nov 1945 Azad Hind Fauj (INA) Trial.
  9. 18–23 Feb 1946 Naval Mutiny.
  10. 24 Mar 1946 Arrival of the Cabinet Mission.
  11. 16 Aug 1946 Direct Action Day.
  12. 2 Sep 1946 Formation of the Interim Government.
  13. 20 Feb 1947 Attlee’s Announcement.
  14. 3 Jun 1947 Mountbatten Plan.

Lahore Resolution, August Offer and Individual Satyagraha

  • 22–24 March 1940: the Muslim League’s Lahore session under Jinnah passed the Pakistan Resolution.
  • 8 August 1940: Viceroy Linlithgow announced the “August Offer”; Gandhi rejected it as “completely unacceptable” and began Individual Satyagraha (“Delhi Chalo”).
  • Vinoba Bhave was the first satyagrahi (17 October 1940), then Nehru, and third Patel.

  3. Where and under whom did the League pass the Pakistan Resolution?

    Lahore session, 22–24 March 1940, under Jinnah. p. 59

Cripps Mission and the Quit India Movement (1942)

  • Cripps Mission: to resolve the political deadlock, PM Winston Churchill sent a mission led by Sir Stafford Cripps in March 1942.
  • 7 August 1942: Congress session at Bombay’s Gowalia Tank, presided over by Abul Kalam Azad; Nehru presented the Quit India resolution (drafted by Gandhi, Nehru, Azad).
  • Passed on 8 August 1942; Gandhi gave the slogan “Do or Die”.
  • Morning of 9 August 1942: the government launched “Operation Zero Hour” and arrested Gandhi and other leaders.
  • Gandhi’s biographer, American journalist Louis Fischer, was with him.
Parallel governmentDetails
BalliaLed by Chittu Pandey
TamlukCalled the “National Government”; lasted December 1942 – September 1944
SataraLongest-lasting (till 1945); led by Y.B. Chavan

Azad Hind Fauj (INA) and Subhas Chandra Bose

Azad Hind Fauj (INA)
  • Formed in March 1942 under Mohan Singh, in Singapore; the idea originated with Giani Pritam Singh and Fujiwara.
  • First division formed on 1 September 1942 with Mohan Singh as commander.
  • On 4 July 1943 Ras Bihari Bose handed command to Subhas Chandra Bose.
Subhas Chandra Bose (brief)
  • Born 23 January 1897, Cuttack (Odisha).
  • Stood 4th in the Civil Services in 1920 and resigned; joined Congress in 1921 (inspired by Gandhi).
  • Political guru: Deshbandhu Chittaranjan Das.
  • 1927: formed the Independence League; 1939: resigned the Congress presidency and formed the Forward Bloc.
  • Called “Netaji” by the Germans, “Desh Nayak” by Rabindranath Tagore and “Patriot of Patriots” by Gandhi.

    Singapore, March 1942, under Mohan Singh. p. 60

    4 July 1943. p. 60

    Chittaranjan Das. p. 60

  4. Who called Bose ‘Desh Nayak’, and who ‘Patriot of Patriots’?

    Tagore; Gandhi. p. 60

Wavell Plan, Cabinet Mission, Constituent Assembly and Interim Government

  • Wavell Plan: presented by Viceroy Wavell on 14 June 1945 to resolve constitutional issues.
  • Cabinet Mission: formed by British PM Clement Attlee; reached Delhi on 24 March 1946; members Pethick Lawrence (Chairman), A.V. Alexander, Stafford Cripps.
  • Constituent Assembly: idea first presented at the 1936 Lucknow session of Congress; elections held in July 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
  • Direct Action Day (16 August 1946): on 12 August 1946 the Viceroy invited Nehru to form an Interim Government, which he accepted; the Muslim League opposed it and declared Direct Action Day, leading to riots; Gandhi marched in Noakhali for peace.

Attlee’s Announcement, Mountbatten Plan and the Indian Independence Act

  1. 20 Feb 1947 PM Clement Attlee announced transfer of power by June 1948; Lord Mountbatten appointed Viceroy replacing Wavell.
  2. 24 Mar 1947 Lord Mountbatten became the 34th Governor-General (as per source).
  3. 3 Jun 1947 Partition Plan (Mountbatten Plan) presented.
  4. 4 Jul 1947 Indian Independence Act introduced in the British Parliament.
  5. 18 Jul 1947 Act passed — provided for two Dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947.
  6. 14–15 Aug 1947 Pakistan became independent on 14 August, India on 15 August.
Remember At the time of partition the Congress President was Acharya J.B. Kripalani.

Chapter recap
  • Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution, March 1940 → August Offer (8 Aug 1940) → Individual Satyagraha (Vinoba first).
  • Cripps (Mar 1942) → Quit India (8 Aug 1942) → Operation Zero Hour → parallel governments.
  • INA: Mohan Singh (1942) → Subhas Bose (4 July 1943).
  • Wavell Plan (1945) → Cabinet Mission (1946) → Interim Government (2 Sep 1946) → Attlee (20 Feb 1947) → Mountbatten Plan (3 Jun 1947) → Act (18 Jul 1947).

Commonly confused: August Offer (Linlithgow, 1940) vs Wavell Plan (1945); Cabinet Mission (Attlee, 1946) vs Cripps Mission (Churchill, 1942); Tamluk ‘National Government’ vs Satara (longest-lasting).

Important Events in Indian History (1911–2013)

  1. 1911 King George V visits India; capital transferred from Calcutta to Delhi; Jana Gana Mana first sung at the Calcutta Congress session; first airmail service in India and the world (Bamrauli to Allahabad).
  2. 1919 Dyarchy introduced by the Government of India Act 1919; Rowlatt Act; Jallianwala Bagh tragedy.
  3. 1920 Khilafat Movement; beginning of Non-Cooperation Movement.
  4. 1922 Chauri Chaura outrage (U.P.); suspension of Non-Cooperation.
  5. 1928 Simon Commission’s visit; death of Lala Lajpat Rai.
  6. 1929 Resolution for complete independence at the Lahore Congress session.
  7. 1930 Dandi March; beginning of Civil Disobedience Movement.
  8. 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact; Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru hanged.
  9. 1935 Government of India Act.
  10. 1942 Quit India Movement; formation of Azad Hind Fauj; Cripps Mission’s visit.
  11. 1946 Cabinet Mission’s visit.
  12. 1947 Independence and Partition of India.
  13. 1948 Assassination of Mahatma Gandhi; Pakistan’s first invasion of India.
  14. 1950 India becomes a republic.
  15. 1951 First Five Year Plan; first Asian Games in Delhi.
  16. 1952 First general elections.
  17. 1954 Panchsheel Pact (India–China).
  18. 1956 Linguistic reorganisation of states.
  19. 1957 Decimal system in currency.
  20. 1959 India’s first television service, New Delhi.
  21. 1961 Liberation of Goa from Portugal.
  22. 1962 Chinese invasion of India.
  23. 1964 Death of Jawaharlal Nehru.
  24. 1965 Indo-Pak war.
  25. 1966 Death of Lal Bahadur Shastri.
  26. 1969 Split in the Congress; nationalisation of 14 banks; India’s first nuclear reactor began commercial operation at Tarapur.
  27. 1971 Indo-Pak war.
  28. 1972 Shimla Agreement (India–Pakistan).
  29. 1974 First nuclear test, 18 May, Pokhran (Rajasthan).
  30. 1975 First Indian satellite Aryabhata launched; Emergency declared.
  31. 1977 Congress loses power at the centre for the first time.
  32. 1980 Congress returns to power; nationalisation of six more banks.
  33. 1982 Colour television comes to India; 9th Asian Games in Delhi.
  34. 1984 Death of Indira Gandhi; Operation Meghdoot – full control over Siachen Glacier.
  35. 1991 Death of Rajiv Gandhi; beginning of economic liberalisation.
  36. 1992 Demolition of Babri Masjid; beginning of Panchayati Raj.
  37. 1995 Internet enters India.
  38. 1998 Second nuclear test (Operation Shakti).
  39. 1999 Pakistani troops invade Kargil.
  40. 2000 India’s population reaches 1 billion.
  41. 2001 Gujarat earthquake (January); terrorist attack on Parliament (December).
  42. 2002 Godhra incident.
  43. 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
  44. 2008 Chandrayaan-1 sent to the Moon.
  45. 2013 Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) launched towards Mars.

Indian Polity

Constitutional history, the Constituent Assembly, the structure of the Constitution (Parts, Schedules, sources), rights and duties, the Union and State machinery, Centre–State relations, local government, constitutional bodies and key amendments.

Constitutional Development and the Constituent Assembly

Constitutional development under British rule (1773–1935)

A chain of British Acts first regulated the East India Company, then transferred power to the Crown and gradually brought Indians into law-making — many later features of the Constitution grew out of them.

  • Regulating Act, 1773
    • First step to control the affairs of the East India Company in India.
    • Governor of Bengal named Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings).
    • Supreme Court established at Calcutta (Kolkata) — a Chief Justice and three other judges.
  • Pitt’s India Act, 1784 (source also calls it “Act of Settlement”)
    • Political and commercial functions of the Company separated.
    • A new body, the Board of Control, was formed.
    • British Government given full control over the affairs and administration of the Company in India.
  • Charter Act, 1793
    • Company’s trade monopoly in India extended for another 20 years.
    • Members and staff of the Board of Control began to be paid from Indian revenues.
  • Charter Act, 1813
    • Company’s trade monopoly abolished, except trade in tea and trade with China.
    • Christian missionaries allowed to come to India and “enlighten” the people.
    • Local governments were authorised to levy taxes on individuals, with punishment for non-payment.
  • Charter Act, 1833
    • Governor-General of Bengal made Governor-General of India — Lord William Bentinck the first.
    • Attempt to start open competition for selection of civil servants.
    • Governors of Madras and Bombay (Mumbai) deprived of legislative powers.
  • Charter Act, 1853
    • For the first time, legislative and executive (administrative) functions of the Governor-General’s Council separated.
    • 1854 — Macaulay Committee appointed on the civil services.
  • Government of India Act, 1858
    • Governor-General renamed Viceroy of India — Lord Canning the first Viceroy.
    • New post of Secretary of State for India created.
    • A 15-member advisory council (India Council) formed.
  • Indian Councils Act, 1861
    • Indian representatives brought into the law-making process.
    • 1862 — Lord Canning nominated three Indians to the Legislative Council: Raja of Benares, Maharaja of Patiala, Dinkar Rao.
    • Viceroy authorised to issue ordinances in an emergency.
    • Legislative Councils formed in Bengal (1862), North-West (source: “North West Frontier”) Province (1866) and Punjab (1897).
  • Indian Councils Act, 1892 — functions of the Legislative Councils increased; they could debate the budget and put questions to the executive.
  • Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley–Minto Reforms)
    • Size of Central and Provincial Legislative Councils increased; functions widened — supplementary questions, resolutions on the budget, etc.
    • Communal representation for Muslims (separate electorate).
  • Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms)
    • Central and Provincial Legislative Councils could legislate on subjects in their own lists.
    • (Provincial) subjects divided into transferred and reserved.
    • Dual government (dyarchy) and direct elections began.
    • Central Public Service Commission formed in 1926 for recruiting civil servants.
    • Union (central) budget separated from the budgets of the provinces.
  • Government of India Act, 1935
    • Residuary powers given to the Viceroy (Governor-General).
    • Dyarchy ended in the provinces and introduced at the centre.
    • India Council (set up in 1858) abolished.
    • Federal Public Service Commission set up, with Provincial PSCs and Joint PSCs for two or more provinces.
    • Federal Court established in 1937.
Source check Source calls Pitt’s India Act 1784 the “Act of Settlement”; the Act of Settlement is usually dated 1781 (amending the Regulating Act) — doubtful label. Source says councils were formed in the “North West Frontier Province … 1866”; standard texts give the North-Western Provinces in 1886 — likely misprint. Charter Act 1813 text reads “trade in tea and China” and splits “Local governments were created / Authorised the Government to levy taxes” — read as above. “Mumbai” = Bombay (period name).

389 fixed (296 from British India + 93 from princely states). After the Muslim League separated: 299 (229 from Indian provinces + 70 from princely states).

Main features of the Constitution

  • Longest written constitution; borrowed from various sources.
  • Blend of rigidity and flexibility.
  • Federal system with a unitary bias; parliamentary form of government.
  • Balance between parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy (source: “federal sovereignty and supremacy of judiciary”).
  • Integrated (unified) and independent judiciary.
  • Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, Fundamental Duties.
  • Secular state; universal adult franchise; single citizenship.
Unitary featuresFederal features
Strong centre, single constitution, single citizenship, supremacy of constitution (as listed), integrated judiciary, Governors appointed by the centre, All India Services, emergency provisions Dual polity, written constitution, division of powers, supremacy of constitution, rigid constitution, independent judiciary, bicameral legislature

Preamble

The Preamble grew out of Nehru’s Objectives Resolution and states the nature of the State and its goals; it is not enforceable in a court of law.

  • Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946; adopted on 22 January 1947 — it became the Preamble.
  • Key words in sequence: Sovereign → Socialist → Secular → Democratic → Republic.
  • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added three words: Socialist, Secular, Integrity.
  • Justice — social, economic, political. Liberty — of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship. Equality — of status and opportunity.
  • Nature: not enforceable in a court of law.
Influences and famous descriptions
CountryInfluence on the Preamble
USA“We, the people of India”; the concept of a preamble
AustraliaLanguage of the Preamble
FranceLiberty, equality and fraternity
Russia (USSR)Social, economic and political justice
  • “Soul of the Constitution” — Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava and M. Hidayatullah.
  • “Identity card” of the Constitution — Nani Palkhivala.
  • “Horoscope of the Constitution” (birth horoscope) — K. M. Munshi.
Source check Source reads “Nanpalkivala” and “introduction card”; the usual phrasing is Nani Palkhivala’s “identity card”.

Kesavananda Bharati case, 1973Preamble is a part of the Constitution and can be amended

42nd Amendment, 1976Added Socialism, Secularism and Integrity

Chapter recap
  • Largest single source: GoI Act 1935 (federal system, Governor, PSCs, emergency provisions).
  • UK gave parliamentary features; USA rights and judicial review; Ireland DPSP; Canada strong centre; USSR duties.
  • Ninth to Twelfth Schedules were added by the 1st, 52nd, 73rd and 74th Amendments.
  • Preamble: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; ‘Socialist, Secular, Integrity’ added in 1976.
  • Preamble a part of the Constitution? No (Berubari 1960) → Yes (Kesavananda 1973, LIC 1995).

Commonly confused: Ireland (nomination to Rajya Sabha) vs South Africa (election to Rajya Sabha); Eleventh Schedule (Panchayats) vs Twelfth (Municipalities); Part IX (Panchayats) vs Part IX-A (Municipalities).

ArticleProvision

Citizenship Act, 1955 — modes of acquiring citizenship
  1. By birth — born after 26 January 1950 (except children of diplomats and enemy aliens/foreigners).
  2. By descent — born (outside India) after 26 January 1950 to Indian parents.
  3. If either parent is a citizen at the time of birth.
  4. By naturalisation.
  5. By registration.
  6. By incorporation of territory.
Source check Source heading says “Five grounds” but lists six items; items 2 and 3 overlap (descent through either parent). The Act’s standard five modes are birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory.

Fundamental Rights — Part III

Part III guarantees six groups of justiciable rights; Article 32 makes the right to approach the Supreme Court itself a Fundamental Right.

Right to Equality — Articles 14–18
  • Art. 14 — Equality before law (and equal protection of laws).
  • Art. 15 — No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
  • Art. 16 — Equality of opportunity in public employment.
  • Art. 17 — Abolition of untouchability.
  • Art. 18 — Abolition of titles.
  • Equality before law — negative concept: no special privileges; same law for all (source: “derived from USA”).
  • Equal protection of laws — positive concept: equal treatment by law.
  • Rule of Law (A. V. Dicey) — absence of arbitrary power, equality before law, supremacy of law. The Supreme Court has declared Rule of Law part of the basic structure.
Source check Source says equality before law is “derived from USA”; standard texts trace “equality before law” to Britain and “equal protection of laws” to the USA.
Right to Freedom — Articles 19–22
ArticleFreedom
19(1)(a)Speech and expression (includes press)
19(1)(b)Assemble peaceably and without arms
19(1)(c)Form associations/unions (co-operative societies added by 97th Amendment)
19(1)(d)Move freely throughout India
19(1)(e)Reside and settle anywhere in India
19(1)(g)Practise any profession, occupation, trade or business
  • Art. 20 — Protection in respect of conviction for offences: (1) no double punishment for the same offence; (2) punishment only under the law in force when the offence was committed; (3) no self-incrimination.
  • Art. 21 — Protection of life and personal liberty; includes right to privacy (Puttaswamy case, 2017), live with dignity, clean environment, health, travel abroad (after Maneka Gandhi case, 1978), shelter, free legal aid; education under Art. 21A.
  • Art. 21A — Free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 (86th Amendment, 2002).
  • Art. 22 — Protection against arrest: right to know the grounds, to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours, to consult a lawyer.
Exploitation, religion, culture–education and remedies
  • Right against Exploitation (23–24): Art. 23 — prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour; Art. 24 — prohibition of child labour in factories.
  • Freedom of Religion (25–28):
    • Art. 25 — freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion.
    • Art. 26 — freedom to manage religious affairs.
    • Art. 27 — no one can be compelled to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any religion/religious institution.
    • Art. 28 — no religious instruction in educational institutions wholly funded by the State.
  • Cultural and Educational Rights (29–30): Art. 29 — protection of interests (culture, script) of minorities; Art. 30 — right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
  • Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32) — the five writs (see next topic).
Source check Page 64 gives Art. 25 as “Right to Religious Freedom” and Art. 26 as “freedom to profess, propagate and follow religion”; page 79 places profession/propagation under Art. 25 and management of religious affairs under Art. 26 (the correct split).
Fundamental Rights available only to citizens (not to foreigners)
  • Art. 15 — no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth.
  • Art. 16 — equality of opportunity in public employment.
  • Art. 19 — freedoms of speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession.
  • Art. 29 — minorities’ cultural and educational rights.
  • Art. 30 — minorities’ right to establish and administer educational institutions.
Learning aid “15-16-19-29-30” — citizens only (not from source).

Writs — types and scope

WritMeaningIssued against / purposeNot issued against
Habeas Corpus“To have the body” (produce the body)Both private and public authorities; key safeguard of personal liberty—
Mandamus“We command”Public officer, public body, corporation, lower court, tribunal, governmentPrivate individuals
Quo Warranto“By what authority”Illegal occupation of a public officePrivate or ministerial offices
Prohibition“To forbid”Judicial (lower courts) and quasi-judicial authoritiesAdministrative authorities, legislative bodies, private individuals
Certiorari“To be certified / informed”Judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative authorities — to transfer a pending case to itself or quash an order of a lower court; called a “post-mortem” writLegislative bodies, private individuals
Common confusion Prohibition is preventive (stops a case in progress); Certiorari is both preventive and curative (quashes an order already made) — hence “post-mortem”.

    Article 50. p. 80

Fundamental Duties — Part IV-A, Article 51A

  • Taken from the USSR (Soviet) Constitution.
  • Added on the recommendation of the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976) by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 — originally 10 duties.
  • 11th duty added by the 86th Amendment, 2002; currently 11 duties. Duties are non-justiciable.
  1. Respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
  2. Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle.
  3. Uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity.
  4. Defend the country and render national service.
  5. Promote harmony and brotherhood.
  6. Preserve the heritage of composite culture.
  7. Protect the environment.
  8. Develop scientific temper.
  9. Safeguard public property.
  10. Strive for excellence.
  11. Parents/guardians to provide education to children aged 6–14 years.

    Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976). p. 80
