    86th (2002); parents/guardians to educate children aged 6–14. p. 80

  3. From which constitution were the duties taken?

    USSR. p. 70

  4. Are Fundamental Duties justiciable?

    No — they are non-justiciable. p. 80

Chapter recap
  • Citizenship: Arts 5–11; Art. 9 bars dual citizenship; Parliament regulates by law (Art. 11).
  • FR groups: Equality 14–18, Freedom 19–22, Exploitation 23–24, Religion 25–28, Cultural/Educational 29–30, Remedies 32.
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Quo Warranto, Prohibition, Certiorari.
  • DPSP (Part IV) are non-justiciable; grouped socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual.
  • Duties: 42nd Amdt (10) + 86th Amdt (11th), on the Swaran Singh Committee’s recommendation.

Commonly confused: Prohibition (stops pending case) vs Certiorari (quashes order, ‘post-mortem’); Art. 21A (education, FR) vs Art. 45 (early childhood, DPSP) vs 11th duty (parents); Art. 25 (profess religion) vs Art. 26 (manage religious affairs).

Federal system: the Union and its territory (Part I, Arts 1–4)

India is a Union from which States cannot secede, with single citizenship and one Constitution for all States.

  • Art. 1 — India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
  • Art. 2 — Parliament may admit/establish new states (source: “merge any foreign state … with prior permission of the President”). Example: Sikkim became an associate state by the 35th Amendment and a full state by the 36th Amendment (1975) — India’s 22nd state.
  • Art. 3 — Parliament can change the name, boundaries and area of any state.
  • Art. 4 — laws under Arts 2 and 3 amend the First and Fourth Schedules and make consequential provisions (not treated as constitutional amendments).
Source check Source calls Sikkim a “co-state” under the 35th Amendment — the term is “associate state”. The source’s wording of Art. 2 (“foreign state … prior permission of President”) is unclear in source; the Article speaks of admitting or establishing new States.

Merger of the princely states

  • 13 princely states merged with Pakistan.
  • 552 remained in India — task of integration given to Sardar Patel, V. P. Menon and Mountbatten.
  • Three refused to join initially — Hyderabad, Junagadh, Jammu & Kashmir — later merged:
    • Hyderabad — Operation Polo.
    • Junagadh — after a referendum (plebiscite).
    • Jammu & Kashmir — after the Instrument of Accession (merger letter) was signed.

Chapter recap
  • Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) → Nagaur inauguration (2 Oct 1959) → Ashok Mehta two-tier (1977).
  • Singhvi (1986) and Thungon (1988) urged constitutional status.

Commonly confused: Balwant Rai Mehta (three-tier) vs Ashok Mehta (two-tier); 243ZD (District Planning) vs 243ZE (Metropolitan Planning).

Elections, Commissions, Emergency and Language

Election Commission of India (Art. 324)

  • Autonomous constitutional body conducting Union and State elections; established 25 January 1950.
  • Conducts elections to Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Assemblies, and of the President and Vice-President.
  • No role in Panchayat and Municipal elections — a separate State Election Commission handles these.
Article (Part XV, 324–329)Provision
324Superintendence, direction and control of elections vested in the Election Commission
325No one excluded from the electoral roll on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex
326Lok Sabha and Assembly elections on adult suffrage
327Parliament’s power to legislate on elections to legislatures
328State Legislature’s power to legislate on its own elections
329Bar on interference by courts in electoral matters

  4. Which Article bars courts from interfering in electoral matters?

    Article 329. p. 73

Delimitation Commission

  • Appointed by the President; fixes boundaries of constituencies throughout the country; works with the Election Commission.
  • Members: a retired Supreme Court judge (Chairman), the Chief Election Commissioner, and the State Election Commissioners of the respective states.
  • Its orders cannot be challenged in any court.
  • Constituted 4 times: 1952, 1963, 1972, 2002.

Emergency provisions (Part XVIII, Arts 352–360)

Taken from the Government of India Act, 1935; three kinds of emergency.

TypeGroundsApprovalDuration
National Emergency (Art. 352)War, external aggression, armed rebellion; written Cabinet recommendation mandatorySpecial majority6 months, extendable indefinitely; Fundamental Rights may be suspended except Arts 20 and 21
President’s Rule (Art. 356)Failure of constitutional machinery in a stateSimple majority6 months, maximum 3 years
Financial Emergency (Art. 360)Threat to financial stabilitySimple majorityIndefinite, until revoked
  • 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion”.

Chapter recap
  • ECI (Art. 324, 25 Jan 1950) runs Union and state legislature elections; State Election Commissions run local polls.
  • Delimitation Commission: appointed by the President; orders cannot be challenged; 1952, 1963, 1972, 2002.
  • PSCs: Arts 315–323; UPSC costs charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
  • Emergencies: 352 (special majority; Arts 20–21 never suspended), 356 (max 3 years), 360 (until revoked).
  • Eighth Schedule: 22 languages; added by 21st (1), 71st (3), 92nd (4) Amendments.

Commonly confused: Art. 352 (special majority) vs Arts 356/360 (simple majority); 71st Amendment (Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali) vs 92nd (Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali).

Indian Geography

Physical divisions (Himalaya, plateau, hills, coasts, islands), drainage, location and boundaries, soils and agriculture, and India’s minerals, energy and industries — mostly as ordered lists and pairings.

Physiography — Himalaya, Hills, Plateau, Coasts and Islands

Himalaya — divisions, sequence and regional classification

From north to south the Himalaya is a series of parallel belts separated by major thrust faults; Burrard divided it west–east by the rivers that cut across it.

  • North–south divisions: (1) Trans Himalaya, (2) Greater Himalaya, (3) Lesser or Himachal Himalaya, (4) Outer or Shivalik Himalaya.
  • Sequence with thrusts:
    Trans HimalayaITSZGreat HimalayaMCTLesser HimalayaMBTShivalikHFFIndo-Gangetic Plain
  • Trans Himalaya ranges (N→S): Karakoram → Ladakh → Zanskar → Kailash.
  • Ranges of the north-west, N→S (p.82, given twice): Karakoram → Ladakh → Zanskar → Pir Panjal.
  • Lesser Himalayan ranges: Pir Panjal — longest range of the Middle Himalaya (J&K); Dhauladhar — Himachal Pradesh; Mussoorie — Uttarakhand; Mahabharat — Nepal.
Regional division (Sidney Burrard)Between riversLength
Punjab HimalayaIndus – Sutlej560 km
Kumaon HimalayaSutlej – Kali320 km
Nepal HimalayaKali – Teesta800 km
Assam HimalayaTeesta – Dihang750 km
Learning aid West→east “P-K-N-A” (Punjab, Kumaon, Nepal, Assam); river boundaries I-S-K-T-D (Indus, Sutlej, Kali, Teesta, Dihang) (not from source).
Source check Source spells Zanskar as “Zaskar/Jaskar”. Abbreviations as in source: ITSZ = Indus–Tsangpo Suture Zone, MCT = Main Central Thrust, MBT = Main Boundary Thrust, HFF = Himalayan Frontal Fault.

Chapter recap
  • Himalaya, north → south: Trans → Greater → Lesser → Shivalik, separated by ITSZ, MCT, MBT and HFF.
  • Burrard’s west → east regions: Punjab (Indus–Sutlej), Kumaon (Sutlej–Kali), Nepal (Kali–Teesta, longest 800 km), Assam (Teesta–Dihang).
  • K2 (8611 m) tops India’s peaks; Anai Mudi (2695 m) is the highest of South India.
  • The Peninsular Plateau is a triangle bounded by Aravalli/Delhi, Rajmahal, Gir, Cardamom and Shillong–Karbi-Anglong, averaging 600–900 m.
  • Ordered lists to master: Garo → Khasi → Jaintia → Mikir; Nilgiri → Anamalai → Cardamom; Thal → Bhor → Palghat → Shenkottai.
  • West coast: Konkan → Canara → Malabar; east coast: Utkal → Northern Circars → Coromandel.

Commonly confused: Kashmir Valley (Great Himalaya–Pir Panjal) vs Kullu Valley (Dhauladhar–Pir Panjal); Kanchenjunga’s height 8586 m (p.84) vs 8,598 m (p.87); Nilgiri’s Doda Betta (2637 m) vs Anamalai’s Anai Mudi (2695 m).

Chapter recap
  • Ganga – Gangotri, Yamuna – Yamunotri (glaciers); Godavari – Trimbakeshwar, Krishna – Mahabaleshwar; Narmada – Amarkantak.
  • Ganga: most tributaries join from the left (Ramganga … Kosi); right bank only Yamuna, Tons, Son.
  • Indus: Punjab rivers (Jhelum, Chenab, Beas, Ravi, Sutlej) and Zanskar from the left; Shyok, Gilgit, Gomal, Kabul from the right.
  • Peninsular river lengths: Godavari > Krishna > Narmada > Mahanadi > Kaveri.
  • Falls to anchor: Chitrakot (Indravati), Jog (Sharavathi), Dhuandhar (Narmada), Shivasamudram (Kaveri).
  • Lakes: Chilika (largest saltwater lagoon), Loktak (Keibul Lamjao), Kolleru (Krishna–Godavari), Gurudongmar (highest).

Commonly confused: tributary vs distributary (Hooghly); Kapildhara vs Dhuandhar (both Narmada — Amarkantak vs Jabalpur); Dudhsagar on the Mandovi vs Gokak on the Ghataprabha.

Location, Boundaries, Sea Routes, Ports and Hill Stations

Indian Standard Time (IST)

  • Calculated from the 82°30′ E meridian, which passes through Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh).
  • IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT; there is only one standard time for the whole of India.
  • Longitudes determine local time relative to GMT — a difference of 1 hour for every 15° of longitude.
  • Earlier, Mumbai and Kolkata kept their own local times; these were abolished after independence and one standard time adopted.
  • By international understanding, standard meridians are chosen in multiples of 7°30′.
Remember 82°30′ = 11 × 7°30′, and 82.5° ÷ 15° = 5.5 hours ahead of GMT.

    Mumbai and Kolkata. p. 83

Chapter recap
  • IST: 82°30′ E through Mirzapur; 82.5° ÷ 15° = GMT + 5 h 30 min.
  • Border lengths: Bangladesh (longest) > China > Pakistan > Nepal > Myanmar > Bhutan > Afghanistan (shortest, Ladakh only).
  • Channels: 8° (Maldives–Minicoy), 9° (Lakshadweep–Minicoy), 10° (Andaman–Nicobar), Great Channel (Nicobar–Sumatra).
  • 13 major ports; Tamil Nadu has 3; Maharashtra has the most minor ports (53).
  • Port superlatives: Chennai oldest, Visakhapatnam deepest, Nhava Sheva most modern, Mumbai largest.

Commonly confused: 8° vs 9° Channel — 9° is the northern one (Lakshadweep–Minicoy); Duncan Passage (South–Little Andaman) vs Coco Strait (Coco Islands–North Andaman); Palk Strait vs Gulf of Mannar.

Chapter recap
  • Black (regur) soil: self-ploughing, rich in lime/iron/magnesia/alumina, poor in phosphate/nitrogen/humus — cotton soil.
  • Laterite: >200 cm rain, lime and silica leached, iron and aluminium oxides left.
  • Red and yellow soil: on crystalline igneous rocks, rich in potash, ~10.6% of area.
  • Kharif (July–October, monsoon) vs Rabi (sown Oct–Nov, harvested Mar–Apr).
  • 2023–24 leaders: Telangana rice, UP wheat/sugarcane, MP pulses/soybean, Gujarat cotton/groundnut, Rajasthan oilseeds.

Commonly confused: laterite “leaching” vs the source’s “deposition”; Jhum (North-East) vs Podu (Andhra Pradesh) vs Bewar (Bundelkhand); rice leader Telangana vs wheat leader Uttar Pradesh.

Chapter recap
  • Coal by carbon: anthracite (90–95%) > bituminous (55–80%, Gondwana) > lignite (40–55%) > peat (<40%).
  • Raniganj is the oldest coalfield, Jharia the largest.
  • Tarapur (1969) was the first nuclear station; Rawatbhata had Canadian help.
  • Steel plants: Bhilai 1955 (USSR) → Rourkela 1959 (Germany) & Durgapur 1959 (Britain) → Bokaro 1964 (USSR).
  • Digboi (1901, Assam) is the oldest refinery; Paradip (2016) the newest listed.
  • Krishna projects: Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam, Almatti; Sutlej: Bhakra Nangal, Nathpa Jhakri.

Commonly confused: Kakrapar the nuclear plant vs Kakrapar on the Tapi (both Gujarat); BALCO (USSR, Korba) vs MALCO (Italy, Mettur); Bhilai and Bokaro (both USSR) vs Rourkela (Germany).

Chapter recap
  • Origin: Kant (gaseous), Laplace (nebular), Chamberlin–Moulton (planetesimal), Jeans–Jeffreys (tidal), Lemaître (Big Bang).
  • Crust/mountains: Wegener (drift), Holmes (convection), Pratt and Airy (isostasy), Kober (geosynclinal).
  • Discontinuities outward-in: Conrad → Moho → Repetti → Gutenberg → Lehmann.
  • Eras: Precambrian → Palaeozoic → Mesozoic (dinosaurs) → Cenozoic (mammals).
  • Metamorphism pairs: granite–gneiss, limestone–marble, sandstone–quartzite, shale–slate.
  • June solstice: sun over the Tropic of Cancer; December solstice: over the Tropic of Capricorn.

Commonly confused: Moho (crust–mantle) vs Gutenberg (mantle–core); nebular (Laplace) vs gaseous (Kant); Jeffreys appears twice — tidal hypothesis (with Jeans) and thermal contraction.

Chapter recap
  • Atmosphere, bottom → top: troposphere (weather) → stratosphere (ozone, aircraft) → mesosphere (meteors) → ionosphere (radio) → exosphere.
  • El Niño: warm central/eastern Pacific, weak Indian monsoon; La Niña: cool phase, strong monsoon.
  • Cyclone names: cyclone (Indian Ocean), hurricane (Caribbean/Atlantic), typhoon (China Sea, Japan), willy-willy (N Australia), baguio (Philippines).
  • Hot winds: Chinook (Rockies), Föhn (Alps), Sirocco (Italy), Loo (N India); cold: Mistral, Bora, Purga, Blizzard.
  • Tropical grasslands: Savanna, Campos, Llanos; temperate: Prairie, Pampas, Veld, Downs, Steppe.

Commonly confused: El Niño vs La Niña (monsoon weakens vs strengthens); Chinook (hot, Rockies) vs Blizzard (cold, USA–Canada); Halophyte (saline) vs Hydrophyte (water) vs Hygrophyte (swamp).

Oceans — Trenches, Currents, Salinity, Straits, Channels, Canals and Islands

Major ocean trenches

  • Mariana Trench — deepest in the world (11,034 m), east of the Philippines; part of an almost continuous series of trenches along both Pacific margins.
  • Tonga Trench — South Pacific, east of the Tonga Islands.
  • Sunda (Java) Trench — deepest point of the Indian Ocean, south of Java (Indonesia); maximum depth 7,725 m (25,344 ft).
  • Puerto Rico Trench — on the boundary of the Caribbean Sea and Atlantic Ocean.

Ocean currents

OceanWarm currentsCold currents
AtlanticGulf Stream, Brazil, Florida, Irminger, North Equatorial, South Equatorial, Guinea, Norway, North Atlantic DriftCanary, Benguela, Labrador, Falkland, East Greenland, Antarctic

  • Benguela — cold; flows south → north along the west coast of South Africa; source calls it the only cold current of the South Atlantic.
  • Canary — cold; flows north → south off north-western Africa.
  • Peru/Humboldt — cold; along western South America in the south-east Pacific.
  • Gulf Stream — warm; formed where the Florida Current joins the Antilles Current beyond Cape Hatteras; flows along the east coast of the USA; discovered by Ponce de León in 1513.
  • Brazil Current — warm; north → south along the Brazilian coast.
  • Agulhas — warm; north → south in the Indian Ocean.

Chapter recap
  • Mariana (11,034 m) is the deepest trench; Sunda/Java (7,725 m) is the Indian Ocean’s deepest.
  • Source examples: cold currents (Benguela, Canary, Humboldt) on west coasts; warm (Gulf Stream, Brazil, Agulhas) on east coasts.
  • Salinity: Lake Van 330 > Dead Sea 238 > Great Salt Lake 220 ≫ oceans 35; Arabian Sea 36 > Bay of Bengal 30.
  • Suez (1869) links Mediterranean–Red Sea; Panama (1914, 82 km) links Atlantic–Pacific; Kiel links Baltic–North Sea.
  • Gibraltar: Spain–Morocco; Bering: Alaska–Russia; Dover: Britain–France; Palk: India–Sri Lanka.
  • Canada has the longest coastline; India 16th (7,516 km, older figure).

Commonly confused: Golden Triangle (Myanmar–Laos–Thailand) vs Golden Crescent (Iran–Afghanistan–Pakistan); Welland (Erie–Ontario) vs Soo (Superior–Huron); 8° vs 9° vs 10° channels.

Chapter recap
  • Highest peaks: Alps – Mont Blanc; Atlas – Toubkal; Elburz – Damavand; Zagros – Zard Kuh; Tien Shan – Pobeda; Altai – Belukha.
  • Africa: Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) > Mount Kenya > Stanley > Speke > Baker.
  • Deserts by size (source): Sahara → Australian → Arabian → Gobi → Kalahari; Sahara spans 11 countries.
  • Plateaus: Pamir “Roof of the World”, Meseta (Spain), Abyssinian (Ethiopia), Laurentian (Canada).
  • Waterfalls: Angel (highest, Venezuela), Iguazu (largest system), Victoria (Zambezi), Niagara (USA–Canada).

Commonly confused: Angel Falls (highest) vs Iguazu (largest system); Kalahari (Botswana–Namibia–SA) vs Namib (Namibia coast); Elburz (Damavand) vs Elbrus (Caucasus).

Chapter recap
  • Congo crosses the Equator twice; Limpopo crosses the Tropic of Capricorn twice; Niger is the “Oil River”.
  • Europe: Volga (longest, to Caspian), Danube (Black Forest → Black Sea), Rhine (Swiss Alps → North Sea).
  • Lake superlatives: Baikal oldest/deepest, Caspian largest, Superior largest freshwater, Titicaca highest navigable, Dead Sea lowest.
  • Nile dams: Owen Falls (White Nile), Sennar (Blue Nile), Aswan; Zambezi: Kariba, Cahora Bassa.
  • Khartoum sits at the White Nile–Blue Nile confluence.

Commonly confused: largest lake Caspian vs “Baikal” (source conflict); Lake Superior (largest freshwater by area) vs Baikal (oldest, deepest); Volga (Caspian) vs Danube (Black Sea).

General Science

Physics — Laws, Units, Quantities and Energy Conversion

Important laws of science

Pascal’s law
Pressure applied anywhere in a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid (in equilibrium, liquid pressure is equal on all sides). Applications: hydraulic lift, hydraulic press, hydraulic brake.
Hooke’s law
Within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain. Young’s modulus indicates the stiffness of a solid, i.e. its resistance to deformation.
Boyle’s law
At constant temperature, the volume of a given quantity of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.
Archimedes’ principle
The upthrust on a body immersed in a fluid equals the weight of fluid displaced. Used in hydrometers, ships and submarines.
Source check Source says Young’s modulus tells “the stiffness of the skin” — a mistranslation of “solid/body”.

Newton’s three laws of motion

Published by Sir Isaac Newton in Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), 1687.

  1. First law (inertia) — a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts on it.
  2. Second law — rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and occurs in its direction: F = ma.
  3. Third law (action–reaction) — every action has an equal and opposite reaction; e.g. recoil of a gun when firing, a rocket moving forward.

  • Pascal (hydraulics), Hooke (stress ∝ strain), Boyle (V ∝ 1/P at constant T), Archimedes (upthrust = weight displaced).
  • Newton (Principia, 1687): inertia → F = ma → action–reaction.
  • Surface tension: spherical raindrops, floating needle, kerosene on larvae, soap bubbles.

Electromagnetic Waves, Light and Sound

Electromagnetic waves — ranges, order, discoverers and uses

Wave (increasing wavelength)Wavelength (approx.)Discoverer (as per source)Uses
Gamma rays< 10 picometresBecquerelDestroying cancer cells (medicine)
X-rays0.01 – 10 nmRöntgenDiagnosis and treatment; viewing bones and internal organs
Ultraviolet10 – 400 nmRitterWater purifiers (killing microbes)
Visible light400 – 700 nmNewton—
Infrared700 nm – 1 mmHerschelRemote controls (TV), treatment of patients, AC systems
Microwaves1 mm – 1 m—Radar, satellite communication, weather forecasting, microwave ovens, mobile phones, Wi-Fi
Radio waves> 1 mShort waves — Heinrich Hertz; long waves — MarconiBroadcasting (radio, TV), telecommunication, mobile phones

  • Decreasing energy/frequency: gamma → X-rays → ultraviolet → visible → infrared → microwave → radio.

Phenomena of light

PhenomenonExamples
RefractionObject/fish in water appears shallower; bottom of a vessel or pond (swimming pool) appears raised; Sun visible before actual sunrise and after sunset; Sun looks flattened/oval at sunrise and sunset; twinkling of stars; rainbow; movie projector; prism
ReflectionFace in a mirror; image in still water; light returning from a shiny surface; kaleidoscope; flashlight
Total internal reflectionBrilliance (shining) of diamond; optical fibres; mirage (in deserts and in cold regions); endoscope; cracked glass appearing shiny; air bubble in water shining; soot-coated ball shining in water
InterferenceColours of soap bubbles, oil film on water, CD
ScatteringBlue sky; blue sea; red Sun at sunrise/sunset; danger signals are red because red scatters least
  • Increasing wavelength of visible colours: Violet → Blue → Green → Yellow → Orange → Red.
  • Decreasing frequency: Red → Orange → Yellow → Green → Blue → Violet (as printed in source — note this list actually runs in increasing frequency).
  • Light intensity is measured by a photometer.
Source check p.130 heads the list “Red → … → Violet” as “Decreasing Frequency Order”; red has the lowest frequency, so this order is increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength).

Sound — characteristics, types and speed

Wavelength
Distance travelled by a wave before it repeats.
Amplitude
Maximum displacement of particles; higher amplitude = louder sound.
Frequency
Waves per second; higher frequency = higher pitch.
Time period
Time to complete one cycle.
Velocity
Speed at which the wave travels.
TypeMeaning
InfrasonicFrequency below 20 Hz — below human hearing
UltrasonicFrequency above 20,000 Hz — beyond human hearing
SubsonicMoving slower than sound
SupersonicMoving faster than sound (above Mach 1)
HypersonicSpeed of Mach 5 and above (source: “5.0–100”)
  • Speed of sound at 25 °C: solid > liquid > gas; maximum in aluminium (6420 m/s); aluminium > nickel > steel > iron > brass; glass > water > hydrogen > helium > air.
  • Uses of ultrasonic waves: sonar; cleaning clothes and watch parts; removing soot from chimneys; ultrasound/sonography (source also says ECG); killing insects; locating hidden objects; automatic doors; heating liquids.
Test your memory

  1. What frequency defines ultrasonic and infrasonic sound?

    Ultrasonic > 20,000 Hz; infrasonic < 20 Hz. p. 123

    Supersonic — moving faster than sound (above Mach 1); ultrasonic — frequency above 20,000 Hz. p. 123

  3. In which listed medium is sound fastest at 25 °C, and at what speed?

    Aluminium, 6420 m/s. p. 130

  4. Which property of a sound wave decides loudness, and which pitch?

    Amplitude — loudness; frequency — pitch. p. 122

  5. Hypersonic speed starts at what Mach number?

    Mach 5. p. 123

Chapter recap
  • EM spectrum by decreasing wavelength: radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma (energy rises the other way).
  • Refraction: twinkling stars, early sunrise, raised pond bottom; TIR: diamond, optical fibre, mirage; scattering: blue sky, red danger signals.
  • Concave lens corrects myopia, convex lens hypermetropia; concave mirror — headlights, shaving; convex mirror — rear-view.
  • Infrasonic < 20 Hz < audible < 20,000 Hz < ultrasonic; subsonic < Mach 1 < supersonic < Mach 5 ≤ hypersonic.
  • Sound travels fastest in solids (aluminium 6420 m/s), slowest in gases.

Commonly confused: ultrasonic (frequency) vs supersonic (speed); convex lens vs convex mirror uses (source mixes them); visible colours Red → Violet is increasing frequency despite the source’s label.

Chapter recap
  • LPG = butane + propane; CNG = methane + ethane; water gas = CO + H₂; biogas = methane.
  • Natural acids: vinegar–acetic, curd–lactic, tamarind–tartaric, ant sting–formic; aqua regia = HNO₃ + HCl.
  • Sodium compounds: washing soda Na₂CO₃, baking soda NaHCO₃, caustic soda NaOH, hypo Na₂S₂O₃.
  • Alloys: brass Cu+Zn, bronze Cu+Sn, solder Sn+Pb, stainless steel Fe+Cr+Ni.
  • Particles: electron (Thomson), proton (Rutherford), neutron (Chadwick); periodic table Mendeleev → Moseley.
  • Medical isotopes: I-131 thyroid, Co-60 cancer, Na-24 clots, P-32 leukaemia.

Commonly confused: washing soda (Na₂CO₃) vs baking soda (NaHCO₃); Plaster of Paris (½H₂O) vs gypsum (2H₂O); brass (zinc) vs bronze (tin); crown vs flint glass (source conflict).

Biology — Cell, Classification and the Human Body

The cell and its organelles

Schleiden and Schwann’s cell theory (1838–39): all organisms are made of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life.

OrganelleNickname / function
NucleusControl centre of all cell activities
MitochondriaPowerhouse (energy house) of the cell — produces ATP
Ribosome“Factory of protein” — protein synthesis
Chloroplast“Kitchen of the cell” — photosynthesis; “cell within a cell”
LysosomeSuicide bag — enzymes destroy useless or harmful components
Golgi bodies“Traffic police” of the cell — synthesise, store and transport substances
Endoplasmic reticulumSynthesises proteins and lipids; rough and smooth ER
ChromosomeCarrier of hereditary traits
Cell membraneOuter semi-permeable layer controlling entry and exit of substances
CytoplasmJelly-like substance containing the organelles
  1. 1831 Robert Brown discovered the nucleus.
  2. 1838–39 Schleiden and Schwann — cell theory.
  3. 1869 Friedrich Miescher discovered DNA.
  4. 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick — double-helix model of DNA.
Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells
ProkaryoticEukaryotic
NucleusNo true nucleus; DNA in a nucleoid without membraneTrue nucleus with nuclear membrane; DNA organised as chromosomes
SizeSmall, 1–10 µmLarge, 10–100 µm
DNACircular, not organised into chromosomesLinear chromosomes
OrganellesNo membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, Golgi, ER)Mitochondria, Golgi bodies, ER (rough and smooth), lysosomes etc.
RibosomesSmall, 70SLarge, 80S
Cell wallUsually present; peptidoglycan in bacteriaPlants — cellulose; fungi — chitin; animals — none
DivisionBinary fissionMitosis and meiosis
OtherSemi-permeable membrane; flagella (cilia) for movement—
ExamplesBacteria and ArchaeaPlants, animals, fungi, protists
Source check Source prints prokaryotic ribosomes as “705”; it means 70S.

Facts about animals

  • Mammals — three subclasses:
    • Prototheria — lay eggs; e.g. echidna, platypus.
    • Metatheria — give birth to immature young that develop in a pouch (marsupium); e.g. kangaroo.
    • Eutheria — give birth to fully developed young; e.g. humans.
  • Goat has the highest blood temperature among mammals (average 39 °C) — as per source.
  • Duck-billed platypus — “only poisonous mammal” (as per source).
Animal classHeart chambers
Fishes2
Amphibians3
Reptiles3 (exception: crocodiles have 4)
Birds4
Mammals4
Source check “Massupial” = marsupium (pouch). The platypus is not the only venomous mammal (some shrews and solenodons are venomous) — doubtful superlative.

Human brain and blood groups

Human brain
  • Three parts — fore-brain, mid-brain, hind-brain; brain + spinal cord = central nervous system.
  • Fore-brain — main thinking part; controls voluntary actions; processes sensory information from ears, eyes, nose, tongue, skin.
  • Mid-brain — small central part of the brain stem; relays signals.
  • Hind-brain — controls heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, sleep, walking etc.
  • Brain stem — connects fore-brain to spinal cord; includes (as per source) the cerebellum, pons and medulla oblongata.
  • Cerebellum — balance, equilibrium and posture (walking, riding).
Blood groups
  • Discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901, who classified four groups (A, B, AB, O) from antigens and antibodies; Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1930.
GroupAntigenAntibodyNote
AAAnti-B—
BBAnti-A—
ABA and BNoneUniversal recipient — can receive from any group
ONoneAnti-A and anti-BUniversal donor — can donate to any group but receive only O

Chapter recap
  • Organelles: mitochondria (powerhouse), lysosome (suicide bag), ribosome (protein factory), Golgi (traffic police), chloroplast (kitchen).
  • Prokaryotes: no true nucleus, 70S ribosomes, binary fission; eukaryotes: nucleus, 80S, mitosis/meiosis.
  • Five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia; plants: thallophyta → bryophyta → pteridophyta → gymnosperms → angiosperms.
  • Mammals: Prototheria (eggs), Metatheria (pouch), Eutheria; hearts: fish 2, amphibians/reptiles 3, birds/mammals 4.
  • Blood groups (Landsteiner, 1901): O universal donor, AB universal recipient.

Commonly confused: 70S (prokaryote) vs 80S (eukaryote); universal donor O vs universal recipient AB; cerebellum (balance) vs fore-brain (thinking).

Plant Science and Agriculture

Plant hormones

HormoneFunctions (as per source)
AuxinsCell elongation and division; control plant movements; prevent leaf fall; seedless (parthenocarpic) fruits — pea, wheat, barley, cotton, tomato, potato; high concentration promotes stem growth, low concentration root growth; kill dicot weeds; prevent lodging
GibberellinsQuick seed germination; increase height of dwarf plants; widen leaves; promote stem and root growth; induce flowering and parthenocarpic fruits
CytokininsIncrease cell division; protein synthesis; growth of lateral buds; control organ formation; keep leaves green (prevent chlorophyll breakdown); inhibit root system
EthyleneRipening of fruits; abscission of leaves, flowers, fruits
Abscisic acid (ABA)Growth inhibitor — stops cell division; promotes leaf fall (defoliation); controls opening/closing of leaves and flowers (stomata)
FlorigenInduces flowering
Source check Source writes “Abscissic acid (ABC)” (= abscisic acid, ABA).

Insectivorous plants

They grow where nitrogen is lacking (source: “nitrogen is absent in insectivorous plants”); to meet the deficiency they attract insects by scent and digest them. Examples: pitcher plant (Nepenthes), sundew (Drosera), Venus flytrap (Dionaea), Sarracenia, bladderwort (Utricularia).

Economy

Unemployment, poverty lines, inflation-control tools, money supply, banking terms, plans and schemes, and Census 2011 figures.

Unemployment, Poverty & Inequality

5 types — know the sector!

Types of unemployment

Unemployment is classified by its cause. The source lists five types twice (p. 137 and p. 138); both descriptions are merged below.

TypeCause / meaningWhere found / note
FrictionalThe period between leaving one job and getting another; also caused by technological changes, e.g. layoffs.Called "search" or "voluntary" unemployment. Found in developed countries.
StructuralLack of skills / qualifications; not getting work matching one's requirement.Found the most in India.
DisguisedMore people engaged in a work than required; removing them leaves production unchanged.Marginal productivity = zero. Especially in the agricultural / unorganised sector.
SeasonalCaused by weather/season — work during the season, unemployed for the rest of the year.Especially in the agricultural sector.
CyclicalCaused by inflation or recession; lack of demand in a recession, ends when demand rises.Mostly in developed countries; its statistics are negligible in India.
Remember In India, the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) collects and publishes employment and unemployment data.
Common confusion Disguised (extra workers, zero marginal productivity) vs Seasonal (no work in the off-season) — both are typical of agriculture.

    Frictional. p. 137

  4. Which organisation collects India’s employment and unemployment data?

    NSSO (National Sample Survey Organisation). p. 137

  5. Cyclical unemployment is caused by what?

    Recession/inflation — lack of demand; ends when demand rises. p. 137

Committees for poverty measurement

  1. 1979 Alagh Committee — poverty measured on the basis of nutrients; norm fixed at 2400 kcal (rural) and 2100 kcal (urban).
  2. 1993 Lakdawala Committee — state-specific poverty lines; to be updated using CPI-IW in urban areas and CPI-AL in rural areas.
  3. 2009 Tendulkar Committee — poverty line: Rs 1,000 per person per month (urban), Rs 816 (rural).
  4. 2014 Rangarajan Committee — all-India: Rs 972/month (₹32/day) rural; Rs 1,407/month (₹47/day) urban.

Important curves of economics

CurveWhat it shows
Lorenz curveInequality of wealth and income.
Gini coefficientMeasures income inequality using the Lorenz curve.
Kuznets curveAs GDP rises, economic inequality first increases, then decreases after a point (inverted U).
Environmental Kuznets curveAs GDP rises, environmental damage first increases, then decreases after a point (inverted U).
Phillips curve (source: "Thomson/Phillips curve")Inverse relationship: unemployment falls when inflation rises.
Laffer curveTax revenue rises with tax rates up to a point, then declines (inverted U).
Learning aid Three inverted-U curves: Kuznets, Environmental Kuznets, Laffer — "KEL bends down".

Chapter recap
  • Five unemployment types: frictional, structural (most in India), disguised (MP = 0), seasonal, cyclical; NSSO collects data.
  • Poverty committees: Alagh 1979 (calories) → Lakdawala 1993 → Tendulkar 2009 → Rangarajan 2014 (Rs 972 rural / Rs 1,407 urban).
  • Global MPI (UNDP + OPHI, 2010): health, education, standard of living — 10 indicators.
  • Inverted-U curves: Kuznets, Environmental Kuznets, Laffer; Phillips = inflation–unemployment trade-off.

Commonly confused: disguised vs seasonal unemployment (both agricultural); Lorenz curve vs Gini coefficient; Kuznets (inequality) vs Environmental Kuznets (pollution).

Key banking terminology

Liability
What the bank must pay back in future — e.g. deposits, various savings/small-savings schemes, money borrowed by the bank.
Bank Rate
Rate at which RBI gives long-term loans to commercial banks.
Repo Rate
Rate at which RBI gives short-term loans to commercial banks.
Reverse Repo Rate
Rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks.
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
Part of total deposits banks keep with RBI.
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
Part of total deposits banks keep with themselves.
Common confusion CRR is held with RBI; SLR is held by the bank itself. Bank rate = long-term lending; repo = short-term lending.
Test your memory

  1. Repo rate vs bank rate — what is the difference?

    Both are RBI lending rates to banks: repo — short-term; bank rate — long-term. p. 138

  2. What is the reverse repo rate?

    Rate at which RBI borrows from commercial banks. p. 138

  3. Where is CRR kept, and where SLR?

    CRR — with RBI; SLR — with the bank itself. p. 138

  4. Give two examples of a bank’s liabilities.

    Deposits; money borrowed by the bank (also small-savings schemes). p. 138

Four measures of money supply in India: M1, M2, M3, M4

Liquidity falls as you move from M1 to M4.

M1 most liquidM2M3 "broad money"M4 least liquid
MeasureCompositionNotes
M1 (Narrow money)Cash in circulation (notes, coins) + demand deposits (bank current and savings accounts) + other withdrawable deposits (e.g. bank transfers, demand drafts)Most liquid; directly usable money.
M2M1 + post office savings depositsSlightly less liquid, still easily converted to cash.
M3 ("Broad money")M1 + long-term bank deposits (fixed deposits withdrawable only after a set period)Less liquid than M1 and M2.
M4M3 + other (long-term) post office deposits, e.g. time depositsBroadest measure; least liquid — includes deposits not immediately convertible to cash.

    M1 — narrow; M3 — broad money. p. 140

    Post office savings deposits. p. 140

    M3 + other (long-term) post office deposits. p. 140–141

  4. Which measure is most liquid and which least?

    M1 most; M4 least. p. 140–141

Important facts about the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)

  • India's central bank, established 1 April 1935 on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission.
  • Nationalised: 1 January 1949.
  • Main objectives: control currency, regulate the banking system, ensure financial stability.
  • RBI's monetary policy plays an important role in controlling inflation and inflationary pressure.
  • Repo and reverse repo rates are set by RBI, which controls cash flow in the banking system.
  • First Governor: Osborne Smith.
  • First Governor of independent India: C. D. Deshmukh.
  • Current Governor (as per source): Shaktikanta Das.
Source check The source names Shaktikanta Das as the current RBI Governor; Sanjay Malhotra succeeded him in December 2024. Verify against current affairs before the exam.

Chapter recap
  • Quantitative tools: repo, reverse repo, bank rate, CRR, SLR, OMO, MSF; qualitative: credit rationing, margin requirement, moral suasion.
  • Repo = RBI short-term lending; bank rate = long-term lending; reverse repo = RBI borrowing.
  • CRR is kept with RBI, SLR with the bank itself.
  • M1 (narrow) → M2 (+ PO savings); M3 broad money (M1 + time deposits) → M4 (+ other PO deposits); liquidity falls.
  • RBI: 1 April 1935 (Hilton Young), nationalised 1 Jan 1949; first Governor Osborne Smith.

Commonly confused: repo vs reverse repo vs bank rate; CRR (with RBI) vs SLR (with bank); M2 = M1 + PO savings, but M3 = M1 (not M2) + time deposits.

Fiscal Terms & Tax Reforms

Important terms: deficits

DeficitDefinition
Budgetary deficitTotal expenditure − total receipts
Fiscal deficitTotal expenditure − (total receipts less borrowings)
Revenue deficitRevenue expenditure − revenue receipts
Primary deficitFiscal deficit − interest payments (i.e. excess of total expenditure over total receipts less borrowings and interest payments)
Remember Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
Test your memory

  1. Define fiscal deficit.

    Total expenditure − (total receipts less borrowings). p. 139

  2. How is primary deficit derived from fiscal deficit?

    Fiscal deficit − interest payments. p. 139

  3. Revenue deficit = ?

    Revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. p. 139

  4. Budgetary deficit = ?

    Total expenditure − total receipts. p. 139

Important terminology related to economics

GDP (Gross Domestic Product)
Total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a given period.
Inflation
Rise in prices of goods and services, indicating a fall in the value of currency.
Deflation
Fall in prices of goods and services; usually occurs during a recession.
Monetary policy
Central bank's policy to influence the economy through money supply and interest rates.
Fiscal policy
Government's policy to influence the economy through taxes and government spending.
Balance of payments
Record of a country's international transactions — exports, imports and financial flows.
Common confusion Monetary policy = RBI (money, interest); Fiscal policy = Government (taxes, spending).

Chapter recap
  • Budgetary deficit = total expenditure − total receipts.
  • Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (receipts less borrowings); primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest.
  • Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
  • Monetary policy (RBI: money, interest) vs fiscal policy (government: taxes, spending).
  • Tax committees: L. K. Jha 1977, Chelliah 1991, Narasimham 1991/1998, Kelkar 2002, Adhia 2016 (GST).

Commonly confused: fiscal vs primary deficit (interest payments); budgetary vs fiscal deficit (borrowings); Chelliah (tax) vs Narasimham (banking) — both 1991.

Planning, Revolutions & Schemes

Major priority areas of the Five Year Plans

PlanModel / priority
First (1951–56)Harrod–Domar model; priority to agriculture.
Second (1956–61)Mahalanobis model; priority to industry. Projects at Bhilai, Durgapur and Rourkela.
Third (1961–66)"Gadgil model"; agriculture and industry. Bokaro Iron & Steel set up in 1964 with Soviet cooperation.
Fourth (1969–74)Growth with stability; removing income inequalities.
Fifth (1974–79)Poverty alleviation and population control.
Source check Source calls Bhilai, Durgapur and Rourkela "hydroelectric power projects"; these are the Second Plan's integrated steel plants.

Environment

Ecology terms and thinkers, biodiversity and its conservation, protected areas, pollution, energy, environmental laws, conventions, climate conferences and SDGs.

Ecology Basics & Terminology

Important environmental terminology

Sustainable development
Using resources while keeping in mind the needs of future generations. Given by the Brundtland Commission (1987) in its report "Our Common Future".
Ecomark
Given by the Bureau of Indian Standards (1991) to environment-friendly products.
AGMARK
Given to agricultural / food products.
Greenwash
Making false promises about environmental protection.
Habitat
The particular place where organisms live.
Lentic habitat
Still-water habitats — ponds, wetlands, lakes.
Lotic habitat
Running-water habitats — rivers, waterfalls.
Niche
The functional role played by an organism in its ecosystem; term given by Grinnell.
Ecosystem
A community of organisms together with the environment in which they live; term used by A. G. Tansley.
Carrying capacity
Maximum number of organisms in an area that the environment can support.
Biomagnification
Entry of heavy metals into the food chain and their increasing concentration at successive trophic levels.
Common confusion Lentic = still (lakes); Lotic = flowing (rivers).

    Heavy metals enter the food chain and their concentration increases at each higher trophic level. p. 146

    Bureau of Indian Standards, 1991, for environment-friendly products. p. 146

InteractionEffectExample

Biodiversity — categories and measurement

Three categories of biodiversity
  • Species diversity — number of different species in a particular area.
  • Genetic diversity — variety of genetic information within each species.
  • Ecosystem diversity — variety of habitats, communities and processes in an area.
Measuring biodiversity: alpha, beta, gamma
LevelMeaningExample
AlphaDiversity within one area/community — number of species thereTotal bird species in a forest
BetaDifference (change in species) between two ecosystems/communitiesDifferences between bird communities of two forests
GammaOverall diversity across all ecosystems of a large region (e.g. a state or country)Total plant species of North India
Learning aid α → β → γ = Within → Between → Whole region.
Test your memory

  1. Name the three categories of biodiversity.

    Species, genetic and ecosystem diversity. p. 145

  2. In the α-β-γ diagram, which measure compares two communities?

    Beta (β) diversity. p. 145, 151

  3. The total plant species of North India illustrates which diversity?

    Gamma (γ) — the whole region. p. 151

  1. Himalaya / Eastern Himalaya
  2. Indo-Burma
  3. Sundaland
  4. Western Ghats

  • Sustainable development was defined by the Brundtland Commission (1987), Our Common Future.
  • Ecosystem — Tansley; Ecology — Haeckel; Biodiversity — W. G. Rosen; Hotspots — Norman Myers.
  • Keystone = few but vital (tiger); indicator = signals change (lichen and SO₂).
  • α diversity is within one area, β between areas, γ across a whole region.
  • India's 4 hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Sundaland, Western Ghats.

Commonly confused: Lentic (still water) vs lotic (flowing water); Father of Ecology in India (Ramdeo Mishra) vs Father of Ecology (E. P. Odum); Green Revolution in the world (Borlaug) vs in India (Swaminathan).

Commonly confused: Biosphere reserve (zoned, includes people) vs national park (strict protection); Manas is both a Natural WHS (Assam) and a biosphere reserve.

Pollution, Ozone & Earth Processes

Biodegradable pollutants

Pollutants that nature breaks down into simple, harmless substances.

  • Household waste (garbage), urine, faeces, sewage
  • Agricultural residues, paper, wood, textiles, cattle dung
  • Animal bones, leather, wool, vegetation

Primary and secondary pollutants

Primary pollutantsSecondary pollutants
Emitted directly from the source into the atmosphere; not formed by chemical reaction.Formed in the atmosphere by chemical reactions among primary pollutants.
  1. Carbon monoxide (CO)

  7. Lead (Pb)
  8. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)
  1. Ozone (O₃) — tropospheric
  2. Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)
  3. Smog (photochemical)
  4. Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)
  5. Nitric acid (HNO₃)
  6. Organic aerosols

Also listed on p. 145: SO₃, SO₄, H₂O₂.

Process of soil erosion

SplashSheetRillGullyStream channel
Splash erosion
Caused by raindrops.
Sheet erosion
Soil starts flowing with water.
Rill erosion
Small, shallow channels form in the soil.
Gully erosion
Rill channels become large and wide — e.g. the ravines ("Khoh-Khadde") of the Chambal valley.
Stream channel erosion
Water flows as a thick, large stream.
Test your memory

  1. Put in order: gully, splash, rill, sheet, stream channel.

    Splash → sheet → rill → gully → stream channel. p. 148

  2. What causes splash erosion?

    Raindrops. p. 148

  3. The Chambal ravines are an example of which erosion?

    Gully erosion. p. 148

Chapter recap
  • Primary pollutants are emitted directly (CO, SO₂, NOx…); secondary ones form in the air (O₃, PAN, smog, acids).
  • Biodegradable pollutants are broken down by nature (sewage, paper, wood, cattle dung).
  • Asbestos → lungs; lead → central nervous system; CO → bloodstream; fluoride → teeth.
  • CFCs (fridges, ACs) and halons (fire extinguishers) deplete ozone.
  • Erosion sequence: splash → sheet → rill → gully → stream channel; Chambal ravines are gully erosion.

Commonly confused: Tropospheric ozone (a secondary pollutant) vs stratospheric ozone layer (protective; damaged by CFCs, halons).

International environmental conferences / agreements

  1. 1972 Stockholm Conference (Sweden) — the "Magna Carta of environment"; UNEP established; 5 June declared World Environment Day.
  2. 1987 Montreal Protocol (Canada) — first international agreement to protect the ozone layer; 16 September declared Ozone Day.
  3. 1992 Rio Conference / Earth Summit (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) — UN Conference on Environment and Development; Agenda 21 approved; UNFCCC established.
  4. 1997 Kyoto Protocol ("Earth + 5") — cut greenhouse gas emissions by 5.2% from 1990 levels.
  5. 2002 Johannesburg (Rio + 10, "Second Earth Summit") — agreed a "World Solidarity Fund" for poverty eradication; focus on sustainable development.
  6. 2010 Cancun (Mexico) — decision to set up a Green Climate Fund of US$100 billion.
  7. 2012 Rio + 20 (Brazil, "Earth + 20") — green economy and sustainable development; draft "The Future We Want"; Zero Hunger Challenge; SDGs first proposed here.
  8. 2021 Climate Adaptation Summit (Netherlands) — source: "established new umbrella fund called International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD)".
Source check IFAD is a UN agency founded in 1977, not created in 2021; at the 2021 summit IFAD launched an adaptation programme. Treat the source line with caution.

Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)

  • Statutory body, established September 2008 under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
  • Works under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; HQ New Delhi.
  • Six regional offices: Delhi, Guwahati, Mumbai, Kolkata, Cochin, Chennai.
  • Structure: a Chairperson and 22 members, one-third of whom must be women.
  • Responsible for food certification in India.
  • Functions: lay down guidelines and standards; grant licences; conduct audits; spread awareness about food safety; maintain records and information; keep the government informed.

  • Chhattisgarh touches UP's southernmost point (Sonbhadra).
  • Sonbhadra borders 4 states: MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar.
  • Saharanpur borders Haryana, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh.
  • Lalitpur is surrounded by Madhya Pradesh on three sides.

Naming, formation and reorganisation of UP

  1. 1834 / 1836 North-Western Province (source gives 1834 in one list, 1836 in another)
  2. 1877 North-Western Province and Oudh ("United Province of Avadh and Agra" in the other list)
  3. 1902 United Province of Agra and Oudh
  4. 1937 United Province (listed on p. 159)
  5. 24 Jan 1950 Named Uttar Pradesh
  6. 1 Nov 1956 Reorganisation
  7. 9 Nov 2000 13 districts separated to form Uttaranchal (now Uttarakhand)
State capital and NCR districts
  • Capital: Agra (from 1836) → Prayagraj (from 1858) → Lucknow partially (from 1921) → Lucknow completely (from 1935).
  • UP districts in the National Capital Region — 8: Meerut, Ghaziabad, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Bulandshahr, Hapur, Baghpat, Muzaffarnagar, Shamli.
Source check The two naming lists disagree (1834 vs 1836; "United Province of Avadh and Agra – 1877" vs "United Province of Agra and Oudh – 1902"). Both versions are shown as in the source.

Economy, Energy & Institutions

Agriculture sector in Uttar Pradesh

  • UP contributes about 8% of India's GDP.
  • Agriculture contributes 26% of the state's GDP; growth of agriculture and allied sectors ≈ 10%.
  • UP ranks third in agricultural exports.
  • UP ranks first in milk production and sugarcane cultivation.

Energy resources in UP

  • UP State Electricity Council formed: 1959.
  • Electricity production order: Thermal > Hydro > Nuclear > Solar.
  • UP Electricity Regulatory Commission: 1998.
  • UP New and Renewable Energy Development Agency (UPNEDA): 1983.
  • NTPC gas-based plants in UP — 3: Auraiya, Aonla, Dadri.
  • Oldest thermal plant: Harduaganj (1942).
  • Only nuclear power station: Narora (Bulandshahr), 1991–92.

Heritage & Culture

Gupta-period temples and inscriptions in UP

Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh
In Deogarh village, Lalitpur. Discovered by Captain Charles Strahan; named by Alexander Cunningham.
Bhitargaon Temple
Kanpur district; built in the Gupta period (6th century); the oldest surviving Hindu temple (as per source).
Dhamekh Stupa
At Sarnath, 13 km from Varanasi; marks the Deer Park (Rishipattana) where Buddha gave his first sermon.
Bhitari Pillar Inscription
Of Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE); found at Bhitari village, Saidpur, Ghazipur.
Source check Source spells the discoverer "Captain Charles Stuhan" — usually recorded as Charles Strahan.

    Deogarh, Lalitpur. p. 158

  2. Whose inscription is on the Bhitari pillar, and where was it found?

    Skandagupta; Bhitari, Saidpur, Ghazipur. p. 158

  3. What does the Dhamekh Stupa mark?

    The Deer Park (Rishipattana) at Sarnath, where Buddha gave his first sermon. p. 158

Region-wise = easy recall

Folk dances of Uttar Pradesh

Two source lists (p. 158 by region; pp. 159–160 alphabetical-style) merged and grouped by region.

Purvanchal and Awadh
  • Natwari — Yadav / Ahir community of Purvanchal.
  • Dhobia (Dhobi) — washermen community, at marriage or childbirth; depicts the livelihood bond of washermen and donkeys.
  • Kathghoda (Kathghodwa) — auspicious occasions; a dancer sits on an artificial horse inside a circle of dancers.
  • Nakataura — at the marriage of boys.
  • Bidesia — when the husband goes abroad.
  • Jogini — Awadh region, on Ramnavami.
  • Chaurasia — Jaunpur.
  • Dhedhiya — Fatehpur; a lamp in a perforated clay pot on the head.
  • Dhinvar — performed by the Kahar caste.
Braj region
  • Charkula — women on Holi, balancing 108 lamps (rows of burning circular lamps) on the head.
  • Jhula (Jhoola) — in temples during Shravan.
  • Raas — famous in Braj.
  • Peacock (Mayur) dance — during Rasleela.
Bundelkhand region
  • Rai — auspicious occasions and Janmashtami (p. 158); after harvest as thanksgiving (p. 160).
  • Ghada — auspicious occasions.
  • Pai Danda — traditional, very popular dance of the Ahir community.
  • Baredi — on Diwali, like Braj's Lathmar Holi.
  • Mohaniya — on Diwali.
  • Diwali dance, Devi dance, Kartik geet — Bundelkhand.
  • Khyal — celebrating the birth of a son.
  • Horse dance — auspicious occasions, with horses.
  • Dhuriya — men dance in Prajapati women's attire.
  • Shaura / Shaira — farmers while harvesting (p. 160).
Sonbhadra–Mirzapur (tribal belt)
  • Karma — Kharwar tribals, on Holi.
  • Shaira — by "primitive society" people (p. 158).
  • Chaular — for good rain and a good harvest.
  • Dharkhari — tribes of Sonbhadra.

Nautanki (folk theatre) — popular in Kanpur, Lucknow and Hathras.

Source check The lists conflict on Rai (Janmashtami vs post-harvest) and Shaira (Sonbhadra-Mirzapur vs Bundelkhand farmers). Both versions are given.

Classical dance of UP: Kathak

  • Kathak is UP's only classical dance.
  • Patronised in the court of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh; linked with the Lucknow Gharana.
  • Ghungroo (ankle bells) are central; rhythms are made by stamping the feet.
  • Renowned dancers: Birju Maharaj, Lachhu Maharaj, Sitara Devi, Rama Devi.
